text: Coffee grown in Mananthavady by Brown was known as ‘Anjarakandy Brown’. Coffee in Shevaroys was pioneered by M.D. Cockburn who established Kannahatty Estate in 1843. On the Nelliampathys, Pardeherry was opened by Arnold in 1860. Attempts to grow coffee near Castle Rock (Goa) proved futile. Introduction was undertaken in Assam, Orissa and Andamans with little success. Records show that as early as 1898, Brodie introduced arabica to the Pamuleru valley in Andhra Pradesh by supplying seeds to local people, but with poor results. Similar introduction of coffee was also made at Sircilla in Karimnagar District (Andhra Pradesh) around the same time with good results. Growth and decline During the 1860s most of the planted coffees were arabica (Old Chicks), which had the bean qualities of the original mokka introduced by Baba Budan. Short’s (1864) modest estimate of the average produce during the period under review was 12 cwt per acre (1525 kg ha) or even higher. Coffee cultivation reached its zenith during the early 1860s. This period also witnessed major outbreaks of pests and diseases. White stem borer posed a major threat to Indian Coffee in 1863. Leaf rust, which probably entered India along with seedlings brought from Sri Lanka(Ceylon), was first observed in an epidemic scale in 1869 (Windly, 1933). Green bug also appeared during this period.

heading: HISTORY AND CURRENT STATUS OF COFFEE INDUSTRY IN INDIA
text: White stem borer posed a major threat to Indian Coffee in 1863. Leaf rust, which probably entered India along with seedlings brought from Sri Lanka(Ceylon), was first observed in an epidemic scale in 1869 (Windly, 1933). Green bug also appeared during this period. Subsequent years saw a rapid decline in production due to the cumulative ravages of these pests and diseases. Uneconomic prices and the gold rush in Wayanad added to the rapid decline of arabica. Yields even on well organised estates fell from 8 cwt to less than 3 cwt. Most of the estates with marginal productivity were soon abandoned. During this period, leaf rust epidemic brought to close the flourishing coffee industry of Sri Lanka. arabica gave way to robusta in Java. In South India, planters made every effort to stem the losses. Silver oaks and dadaps were extensively planted to protect the arabicas from enervation by leat rust and borer attacks. Frantic efforts were made to introduce disease tolerant selections, the first in this series being Coorgs developed by Stanley Jupp (1870). Coorgs soon became susceptible to leaf rust disease. Enterprising planters like Matheson introduced seed from Brazil, Venezuela, Costa Rica and Jamaica, while Brooke Mockett, Hamilton, Jackson, Kent and Brown tried to select and evolve disease resistant arabicas with commercial qualities for large scale plantations.

The two most promising types evolved were Jackson’s hybrid and Kents’ (McDonald, 1930). Kents gradually gained popularity. Robusta was introduced from Indo-China at the close of 19th century for planting in estates at lower elevations. The continuous ravages of pests and diseases along with a steep fall in the price decreased the area under coffee from 1,20,000 ha in 1869 to 72,400 ha in 1941. heading: HISTORY AND CURRENT STATUS OF COFFEE INDUSTRY IN INDIA
text: Coffee cultivation is also instrumental in preserving the precious forest ecosystem in traditional areas while in non-traditional areas coffee was introduced to check podu or shift cultivation and thus to control denudation of forest and also soil erosion. Coffee cultivation is confined mostly to hilly tracts of Western and Eastern Ghats as a well distributed annual rainfall is preferable. The Ghats in Karnataka and Kerala and the northeastern region of the country receive rain from the South-West monsoon while coffee areas in Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh and Odisha get rain from the North-East monsoon. The South-West monsoon is normally active from June to September with heavy showers during July-August. The North-East monsoon is received in spells usually caused by low pressure depressions in the Bay of Bengal during October-December. December to March are normally dry months. Summer showers are important for flowering in coffee and are received during March-April. Certain areas in Tamil Nadu where the North-East monsoon is prevalent, blossom occurs more than once. The genus Coffea comprises of about 100 species, most of which are native to Africa. Of these, only two species viz., Coffea arabica and Coffea canephora var. robusta are cultivated commercially in India and many other countries. Another species, C. fiberica 1s grown to a small extent in a few countries. In India, some indigenous species related to Coffea like Psilanthus bengalensis, P. wightiana, P. travencorensts, Nostolachma khasiana are found occurring in forests of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Meghalaya and Assam. Morphology and growth behaviour of coffee Coffee plants needs a period of three years to grow and develop from seed germination to first flowering and fruiting. It is a perennial plant (lives for many years), a well maintained coffee plant lives more than 80 years. It is evergreen (plants that do not shed their leaves during a specific season) in nature. It has a prominent vertical stem giving rise to horizontal primary branches in opposite decussate manner (where two leaves/branches at each node are arranged opposite to each other and each pair of leaves/branches are at right angles to each other). The primary branches develop several secondaries laterally which in turn give rise to several tertiary and quaternary branches. These are collectively referred to as sub-laterals. In each plant, the lateral branches spread out at right angles to the main stem and Central Coffee Research Institute exhibit either erect, semierect or drooping growth habit.

text: The primary branches develop several secondaries laterally which in turn give rise to several tertiary and quaternary branches. These are collectively referred to as sub-laterals. In each plant, the lateral branches spread out at right angles to the main stem and Central Coffee Research Institute exhibit either erect, semierect or drooping growth habit. Apart from the lateral branches, a number of vertical shoots with upright growth also arise from the main stem. These are known as ‘suckers’ and because of their vertical growth habit like the main stem, the suckers are used in vegetative propagation. Vegetative growth and cropping In case of coffee, the vegetative growth of a particular year determines the cropping wood of the succeeding year (normally once the fruits are produced at a node, the same node doesn’t give crop again). Hence, it is necessary to maintain balance between current year’s cropping branches and vegetative wood through systematic pruning in order to minimize the variations in crop yields between succeeding years. Usually, during a high cropping year the plant tends to produce less number of branches, thus affecting the cropping wood of the succeeding year. Root system A well-developed coffee root system consists of five different types of roots: Central tap root which penetrate to a depth of 45 to 90 cm (1.5 to 3 ft) deep. * Axial roots, generally 4 to 8 in number, that grow up to 60 to 90 cm (2 to 3 ft) with profuse branching in different directions. * Lateral roots often run horizontally in the surface soil and grow up to 1.5 to 1.8 m (5 to 6 ft) from the main stem. * Feeder roots which originate from all the types of roots i.e. tap, axial and lateral roots. ¢ Root hairs which grow on the feeder roots which are mostly found in the surface soil and play a major role in absorption of nutrients. Generally, coffee has a shallow root system, particularly robusta which has feeder roots concentrated very close to the surface of the soil, while arabica coffee produces most of the feeder roots in relatively deeper soil. The spread of the roots depends on the type of soil and cultural practices. A salient feature of coffee leaves, as in the case of some other members of Rubiaceae, is the occurrence of ‘domatia’ which are small openings on the lower surface of leaves in the angles of the veins intersecting the mid-rib. They do not appear to have any specific function. In coffee, stomata (minute openings on the leaf for gas exchange) are present only on the lower surface of the leaves and the number of stomata vary from species to species (10,000 to 17,500 cm?). The stomatal number is negatively correlated to ploidy level with arabica showing less number of stomata compared to robusta. This disease was first identified by a British explorer in East Africa, and the disease quickly spread worldwide due to the increasing coffee trade. As the disease was relatively unknown, no fungicides were available to combat it. Additionally, very limited information was available on the host-pathogen relationship in case of coffee leaf rust disease. In India, efforts were made by the enterprising planters to evolve rust resistant coffee varieties through selection and breeding arabica with other rust-hardy exotic species like Coffea liberica. While systematic selection led to identification of early cultivars such as ‘Coorgs’, ‘Chicks’ and ‘Kents’, comprehensive breeding resulted in development of important hybrids like ‘Hamiltons’, ‘Jacksons’ and ‘Netrakonda’. ‘Kents’ was a superior selection that was the predominant planting material during the 1920s.

Therefore, since establishment of the erstwhile Mysore Coffee Experimental Station (renamed as Central Coffee Research Institute), systematic efforts have been made not only to collect the available variability in the existing plantations but also to introduce collections from exotic sources. Initially, between 1925 and 1940, concerted efforts were made to collect and conserve the available variability through systematic surveys of existing coffee plantations. Eventually, an indigenous germplasm bank comprising of more than 250 collections of arabica and robusta was established at Central Coffee Research Institute (CCRI), that formed the base material for developing early Indian selections. Vegetative propagation techniques Vegetative reproduction is a type of asexual reproduction using the vegetative Central Coffee Research Institute parts such as shoots, leaves, that helps to retain a plant’s unique characteristics. This is a common method that works well for several horticultural trees. Coffee plants can also be propagated successfully by conventional vegetative propagation using stem cuttings and through grafting techniques. Propagation by stem cuttings: Coffee plants produce two types of shoots: horizontal, also known as plagiotropic, and vertical, or orthotropic. The vertical shoots, often referred to as suckers, are ideal for vegetative propagation. Horizontal shoots aren’t suitable because they grow laterally thereby result in and spreading plants. Ce While selecting a site for coffee plantation, careful consideration should be given to altitude, aspect, rainfall pattern, soil type, land slope, presence of shade trees, prevailing temperature in the area, availability of water resources, exposure to wind, and transport facilities. A perennial source of water supply is a critical requirement for growing coffee. Soils rich in humus and organic matter, as well as land with gentle slopes that facilitate good drainage, are preferred. , Altitude and Aspect Coffee comes up well at an altitude of 1000 m to 1300 m but the lower and upper limits of elevation for its cultivation could be 600 m and 1600 m respectively, depending on the latitude and longitude. Under South Indian conditions, where more than 95% of coffee is produced, arabica coffee requires higher elevations between 1000 m and 1300 m, while the robusta coffee can be grown between the elevations 800 m to 1100 m. Locations with a northern or eastern aspect are preferred. Southern and western aspects generally suffer from longer exposure to the sun, especially at lower elevations.

To protect the coffee from afternoon sun, thicker shade should be provided at lower elevations. Exposure to wind Coffee is highly sensitive to wind exposure. Eastern winds from December to February can cause damage to plants. To prevent this, wind belts consisting of tall trees like silver oak should be raised along the estate boundary. Central Coffee Research Institute Preparation of land Clean felling is not recommended when forest land is cleared for coffee planting. Selective retention of desired species of shade trees, without causing excessive overcrowding, yields the best results. The land should be divided into blocks of a manageable size, with footpaths and roads arranged in between. The problem of soil erosion becomes severe on steep slopes lacking appropriate overhead shade.

To mitigate the negative effects of these conditions, the practice of growing coffee under shade trees is advocated. Shade trees play a vital role in maintaining stable soil temperature and moisture levels, protecting the coffee plants from extreme weather conditions like of high exposure and improving soil Fertility. The main advantage of shade trees is their ability to reduce the intensity of sunlight and temperature. Growing coffee under shade prevent excessive evaporation of moisture from the soil and thus combating the effects of drought. Additionally, shade trees protect coffee plants from hailstone damages, high wind velocities and overbearing which can negatively impact coffee production. Shade trees also contribute to the improvement of soil fertility. The fallen leaves from the trees add organic matter to the soil, increasing its nutrient content and supporting the growth of beneficial microorganisms.

Single stem method: training coffee bushes for optimal growth and management The single stem system of training is particularly suitable for coffee cultivation in India, where shade is provided to the plants. In this method, the height of the coffee bush is controlled by a process known as topping or capping. Topping diverts nutrients towards thickening the main stem and primary branches, promoting lateral spreading of the plants. Additionally, coffee plants trained on a Central Coffee Research Institute single stem form a dense ground cover that protects the soil from erosion and minimizes fertility loss. Single stem trained plants exhibit a wellshaped bush framework, making them easily manageable during farm activities such as pruning, spraying with protective chemicals or nutrient solutions, and harvesting. Their uniform height allows for convenient handling and maintenance. Moreover, the balanced structure of single stem trained plants reduces the risk of breakage, distinguishing them from plants trained using the multiple stem system. Light pruning: Encouraging growth and maintaining balance Light pruning in coffee involves the selective removal of various types of branches, such as old, unproductive, criss-cross, lean, lanky, and whippy wood, as well as diseased, damaged, and ground-touching branches. This method is particularly suitable for coffee plants trained on the single stem system. Regular light pruning is recommended as it promotes the growth of new branches that will serve as the next year’s cropping wood. Light pruning is applicable to both arabica and irrigated robusta coffee. However, for unirrigated robusta, light pruning may only be necessary every alternate year. In the fifth year, the second sucker is removed, and a new sucker is allowed, followed by the removal of the third sucker in the sixth year and the substitution with a new sucker. This cycle of pruning and sucker management is practiced in a cyclic manner after the harvest of the crop. By following this sequential sucker management approach, cyclic pruning aims to maintain a balanced and productive framework for the coffee plant. It ensures the timely removal of older suckers and the establishment of new suckers to sustain the plant’s growth and productivity over the pruning cycle. heading: TRAINING, PRUNING, AND REJUVENATION
text: Rejuvenation is a process employed to restore badly damaged coffee bushes, which may have suffered from falling branches during shade regulation or irregular pruning. Collar pruning/ stumping is a rejuvenation technique that can effectively revive such bushes. During collar pruning/stumping, the damaged bushes are cut at a 45-degree angle facing East or North-East, approximately 30 cm above the ground. This procedure is typically performed after the first few summer showers, usually in March-April. To prevent rotting of the cut surface, it is essential to treat the area with Bordeaux paste, which consists of 1 kg of CuSO, and kg of lime dissolved in 4.5 liters of water. However, in the case of old robusta plants, the production of suckers may experience a failure rate of around 20-30%. To induce sucker production, a spray of IAA (Indole-3-acetic acid) at a concentration of 200 ppm, combined with 1% DMSO (Dimethyl sulphoxide) solution, can be applied to the collar-pruned stumps. This solution contains 200 mg of IAA and 10 ml of Dimethyl sulphoxide dissolved in 1 litre of water. By implementing this treatment, vigorously growing suckers can be encouraged to emerge from 2.5 cm below the cut surface. These suckers are then trained to form a single-stem canopy, contributing to the rejuvenation of the coffee bush. Do’s and Don’ts in training and pruning of coffee for lower heights

Soil management involves various operations and practices aimed at improving soil characteristics to create ideal conditions for plant growth. In coffee-growing areas, it is essential to minimize the effects of soil moisture fluctuations through appropriate soil management measures. These practices can be categorized into three main types: soil conservation measures, soil moisture conservation measures, and drainage measures. Soil conservation measures in coffee-growing areas Coffee is often cultivated in hilly regions with high rainfall, which poses a significant challenge such as occurrence of soil erosion. This issue is particularly prevalent in new clearings and exposed areas. To address this problem, two effective techniques like contour planting and terracing are recommended. Central Coffee Research Institute Contour Planting for minimizing soil erosion Contour planting is a technique suitable for areas with a slope of 10-20 percent, which corresponds to a vertical drop of 1020 meters for every 100 meters in length.

heading: PRACTICES
text: To address this problem, two effective techniques like contour planting and terracing are recommended. Central Coffee Research Institute Contour Planting for minimizing soil erosion Contour planting is a technique suitable for areas with a slope of 10-20 percent, which corresponds to a vertical drop of 1020 meters for every 100 meters in length. In contour planting, coffee plants within a given row on a slope are positioned at the same level. The process begins by drawing a vertical line from top to bottom, dividing the slope into two equal parts. Pegs are then placed along this line at appropriate intervals based on the degree of slope. Using a ‘Ghat tracer’ set to a level position, planting points are determined perpendicular to the vertical line, starting from the topmost peg. These points are connected to form contour lines, which serve as the rows for planting. While contour planting helps minimize soil erosion by following the natural contours of the land, it is important to note that this technique may result in lower efficiency in farm operations. text: Terracing is an effective method used to prevent soil erosion on land with a slope exceeding 20 percent. It involves the construction of permanent terraces, which are typically created through manual labour. To establish terraces, the distance between them is marked using 4 ‘Ghat tracer,’ similar to the process used in contour planting. The marked contour lines or rows are then worked upon by loosening the soil and fortifying the terrace edges with stones and boulders. When implementing terracing, it is important to ensure that the subsoil does not come to the surface, as this can affect the stability of the terraces. While terracing requires significant manual labour and initial investment, it offers the advantage of improving work efficiency during farm operations. These fortified terraces effectively minimize soil erosion and provide a stable platform for planting. By utilizing terracing as a soil conservation measure, coffee growers can prevent soil erosion on steep slopes, enhance work productivity, and promote sustainable farming practices. Digging In coffee plantations, digging serves various purposes, including weed suppression and soil moisture conservation. Thorough digging to a depth of 30-45cm is performed in new Clearings towards the end of the monsoon season (October-November). Steep slopes are more vulnerable to erosion, so alternative soil management practices should be considered for such areas. text: In undulating lands, the opening of trenches or cradle pits across the slope after the monsoon season is recommended. These trenches or pits are dug in a staggered manner between the rows of coffee, following the contour of the land. Trenches are typically dug to be 30 cm wide, 45 cm deep, and of a convenient length. Cradle pits, on the other hand, are shorter trenches measuring around to 1.5 meters in length. Trenches and cradle pits serve multiple purposes in coffee plantations. Firstly, they act as mini compost pits, allowing fallen leaves, weed biomass, and dadap loppings to decompose and contribute to nutrient recycling. Additionally, they aid in conserving soil moisture and preventing soil erosion. To maintain their effectiveness, the trenches and pits should be renovated once every 2-3 years by removing the deposits and spreading them near the surrounding plants. Amelioration of soil acidity Soil acidity can be corrected by applying liming material such as Agricultural lime (calcium carbonate), Dolomite (calcium & magnesium carbonate), Slaked lime or Central Coffee Research Institute Hydrated Lime (calcium hydroxide) and Burnt Lime (calcium oxide). Correcting soil acidity using liming material is an essential soil management practice regularly undertaken in coffee plantation to maintain soil fertility and productivity. Agricultural lime and dolomitic lime are the most commonly used liming material in coffee plantations. Burnt lime and slaked lime, despite their higher effectiveness and faster action in neutralizing soil acidity compared to agricultural or dolomitic lime are not commonly recommended for coffee soils as they are caustic in action and can harm the delicate feeder roots of coffee plants and adversely affect soil micro flora and fauna. Determination of purity of liming material The purity of liming material or its effectiveness to neutralize soil acidity is expressed in terms of calcium carbonate equivalent (CCE) or neutralization value (Y% NV) of the material. A liming material with a neutralizing value above 80% is generally considered good. The particle size or fineness of the liming material is another crucial factor that determines its effectiveness. Finer material has a larger surface area and reacts faster when applied to the soil compared to coarser material, which are less effective. The particle size of the liming material is determined using a sieve test. The particle size of the liming material should be such that 80% of the material should pass through 60 mesh sieve. Choice of right liming material Choosing the right liming material depends on several factors such as cost per unit of neutralizing value, purity and fineness. Liming material should have a purity of at least 80% calcium carbonate equivalence (% NY) for better efficacy. To achieve an efficient and quick response the material should be finely powdered so that they come into contact with the soil particles upon application.

heading: NUTRIENT MANAGEMENT
text: A simple yet effective method of fertilizer application in coffee plantations is known as the “drip circle application” — for the purpose of fertilizer application this area specifically refers to the circular soil patch which is about 1 & 1/2 ft to 2 ft around the coffee stem and not the actual “drip circle” which corresponds to the periphery of coffee plant canopy along which the rain drops drip. This method of fertilizer application helps ensure that the nutrients are distributed efficiently to the coffee plants while minimizing nutrient loss. The method - The mulch beneath the coffee plant is swept towards its base. Using a stick or fork the soil around one and a half to two feet away from the main stem is gently disturbed. This creates a suitable area for fertilizer application within the “drip circle”. The fertilizer is uniformly spread in a broad circular band within the designated area. The soil is carefully reworked after the fertilizer application making sure it is well mixed with the fertilizer. Finally the area is covered with mulch creating a protective layer. This method of fertilizer application is highly efficient as it minimizes the risk of nutrient runoff and ensures that the nutrients are available to the coffee plants.

Irrigation plays a pivotal role in robusta coffee cultivation, and helps in plant growth and blossom, the essential factor for good crop. There are two primary irrigation methods employed in coffee farming: sprinkler and drip. The sprinkler system, which emulates rainfall, ensures uniform water distribution, but it may result in water wastage due to evaporation and drift. This method is particularly effective in synchronizing flowering and achieving uniform fruit growth. On the other hand, the drip method, which delivers water directly to the plant roots, enhances water conservation. However, it demands a considerable investment for installation and continuous maintenance. A potential drawback of drip irrigation is that it may cause staggered flowering (sporadic blossom) and non-uniform ripening if proper dry window is not provided after December. Coffee is predominantly grown as a rainfed crop around the globe. Notably, in equatorial regions like South and Central America, where there is no clear distinction between wet and dry periods, irrigation for coffee is typically unnecessary. However, in regions experiencing a single rainfall pattern, such as East and Central Africa and India, irrigation becomes crucial during the 4-6 month dry spells to enhance the plant’s growth and productivity. Being an evergreen plant, coffee requires consistent soil moisture during dry periods, In South Indian coffee territories, the South-West monsoon supplies over 60% of the rainfall from June to September, with the remaining rain occurring during the North-East monsoon period in October to December. A dry period often . follows, typically lasting around 3-4 months from December onwards. There can be extensions to this dry period if the North-East monsoon finishes earlier than expected, like at the end of October. The key limitation to coffee production, especially for the robusta coffee, even in efficiently managed estates, is the extended dry period. Moreover, if blossom rains are delayed beyond March, it significantly impacts coffee production.

Major diseases Coffee Leaf Rust Coffee Leaf Rust (CLR) is also known as ‘orange rust’ and earliest of the major tropical plant diseases reported so far. It is caused by the obligate fungus Hemileia vastatrix Berk. & Br. and is considered as one of the most catastrophic diseases of coffee plant. The disease ruined the economy of Sri Lanka and changed the social habit of coffee drinking to tea not only in the coffee producing country but also in coffee consuming countries during late 18" century. Thus, the disease is placed among the seven major pests and diseases of coffee and is considered to be one of the classic diseases. CLR is originated on wild coffee in South-Western Ethiopia and was identified in 1860. But it was first reported on cultivated coffee in Sri Lanka during 1868. Subsequently, the disease spread to nearby Indonesia and India during 1869. In 1950s and 1960s, the disease spread across West Africa. The disease entered to major coffee growing countries like South America, Central America, Caribbean and Mexico in 1970s-90s. The Hawaii islands which was free from coffee leaf rust till 2019, declared the existence of coffee leaf rust disease during October 2020, by the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Cultural operations The cultural method of disease management is aimed at either reducing the inoculum potential or encouraging the healthy growth of the host plant. Some of the cultural operations generally carried out in coffee plantations are summarized below. Clean harvest and — extended perry-free period: Since the CBB exclusively breeds in coffee berries, extending the period without berries in the field significantly reduces the carryover of infestation, Timely and clean harvesting of the coffee crop is of utmost importance. Ensure that no berries are left out on the plant or on the ground. The use of picking mats during the harvesting time helps to minimize the gleanings. If picking mats are not used, collect the gleanings or sweep them along with the mulch and bury them to a depth of 50 cm in the soil. The collection of leftovers and gleanings after the harvest significantly reduces the infestation level in the next year’s crop. Proper drying: Drying coffee to the prescribed moisture level is essential to prevent the breeding of beetles in stored coffee. To prevent this, dry the infested crop on the estate and use fumigated gunny bags for transportation. When procuring bags from curing houses, ensure that it is sufficiently exposed to sunlight and fumigated. P. citri Morphology and life cycle Adult female mealybugs are wingless and possess an oval body covered with a white mealy secretion. Males, on the other hand, are rare, small, and winged. Reproduction mainly occurs through parthenogenesis (without mating), and each female can lay around 1000 eggs. Planococcus citri lays eggs within an ovisac made of fine wax filaments and the eggs will hatch in about ten days, whereas P. lilacinus does not possess an ovisac, and the eggs hatch shortly after being laid. The first instar nymphs, after hatching, settle in a place for feeding and secrete the characteristic mealy covering over their bodies. Wind dispersal also aids in nymph dissemination. Females go through three nymphal instars, while male nymphs transform into winged adults after the second instar, forming a white cocoon. The entire life cycle is completed in approximately one month. Mealybug populations rapidly multiply during hot weather after the monsoon period, with nymphs and adults migrating from the root zone to the aerial parts of the plants, particularly during summer.

Methods of On-Farm Processing of Coffee Knowledge about structure of coffee fruits would help in a better understanding of different types of processing. The fruit has an outer layer of fruit skin (also known as eXecarp) and immediately below the fruit Skin isa layer of mucilage (mesocarp). The Mucilage is juicy in case of arabica while it is of thick consistency in robusta fruits. The mucilage represents 12% to 20% of the coffee fruit. In arabica, the mucilage content ranges from 12.5% (SIn.9) to 19.5% (SIn.13) while in robusta it is between 13.5% (SIn.1) and 16% (SIn.3). Mucilage content is one of the important elements in the outturn from coffee fruits to green coffee/clean coffee. Following the mesocarp, the endocarp is located which otherwise known as parchment cover.

Following the mesocarp, the endocarp is located which otherwise known as parchment cover. Coffee fruits usually contain two seeds which is embedded inside the parchment cover and the seeds are covered with a wafer-thin layer of “testa or seed coat” (often known as silver skin). All the coffee producing countries in the world, process the coffee in two distinct ways viz., 1) wet processing by which plantation or parchment coffee (also called as ‘Plantation Coffee’ in India) is prepared and ii) dry method by which cherry coffee is prepared. In case of wet method of processing, the fruit skin and mucilage are removed and the coffee beans along with the parchment cover are dried up to a desired moisture level before storage at estate level. The dried parchment coffee is subjected to peeling and polishing at the secondary processing facilities (also known as ‘curing works’) to remove parchment cover and silver skin and to obtain clean coffee. Clean coffee obtained by this process is known as “washed coffee” or “plantation coffee”. The coffee effluent, if discharged into natural water bodies without treatment, pollutes the receiving water bodies by depleting dissolved oxygen present in it. Pollution of natural water bodies will have an adverse effect on domestic users, aquatic life, livestock and coffee processing units in the downstream. The problem of water pollution will be intensified in coffee tracts, as the processing period coincides with the dry season during which the flow in natural water bodies will be at minimum level. The solid waste (i.e., pulp/fruit skin/ Sippae) is not posing much problem, as most of it is returned to plantations after composting or vermi-composting. heading: EFFLUENT MANAGEMENT STRATEGIES FOR ON-FARM COLEEE PROCESSING
text: The studies conducted from time to time on the quantum of effluent generated revealed that around 22,000 to 60,000 liter and 28,000 to 70,000 liter of effluent is generated for every tonne of clean coffee bean of arabica and robusta produced, respectively (in case of arabica, 5,550 kg to 6,000 kg of ripe fruits produces one tonne of clean coffee while in robusta 4,500 kg 5,000 kg of ripe fruits produces one tonne of clean coffee). However, after the introduction of “water recycling mechanism” in the pulper unit by the Research Department of the Coffee Board, the quantum of effluent generated is sizably reduced to 16,500 to 22,000 and 25,000 to 30,000 liter of effluent for every tonne of clean coffee of arabica and robusta produced, correspondingly. Further to the above, following the introduction of “Ecopulper” (a new generation pulper-cum-washer machine), the quantum of effluent generated is further reduced to 4,500 to 6,000 and 6,500 to 7,500 liter of effluent for every tonne of clean coffees of arabica and robusta, produced respectively. The thick effluent released from the washer unit of the ecopulper is mechanically mixed with the pulp (released from the pulper) during the course of coffee processing itself and then discharged to compost pit using screw conveyer. Thus, the effluent generation is almost nil in case of Ecopulper.

This treatment method is basically an anaerobic-cumaerobic digestion method. The basic unit of NEERI ETP model consists of i) one equalization tank, ii) two anaerobic lagoons, iii) one aerobic lagoon and iv) one settling tank. The NEERI-ETP do not require lining of lagoons, as they are made up of size stone masonry construction and thus ensure water tightness and effluent does not percolate into ground water. The steps to be followed for the treatment of coffee effluent following NEERI-ETP unit is detailed hereunder ¢ All the solid materials such as fruit skin, broken wet parchment and parchment cover should be separated from the pulped water and fresh effluent coming out of washer, using suitable screens (screen with 4 mm diameter holes), so as to reduce the pollution load ¢ The coffee effluent coming out of the washer should be stored in a tank/lagoon (called as equalization tank/lagoon) for about one day. The capacity of this lagoon should be of one day’s water use capacity of the processing unit during peak harvesting period The effluent in the equalization tank/lagoon should be neutralized with appropriate amount of liming material (eg., spray lime) to raise the pH of the fresh effluent to neutral range (around 7 pH).

These impurities are to be removed during pre-cleaning and de-stoning process to protectthe curing machinery. The precleaning and de-stoning process starts when the coffee is dumped in to hoppers fitted with perforated metal screens. As the coffee falls through the screens, large impurities such as sticks, straw, string and large pieces of earth are removed. A powerful fan sucks out as muchdust as possible from the hopper while thecoffee falls through the screen. Aspiration is very important in a coffee mill. heading: SECONDARY PROCESSING OF COFFEE
text: As the coffee falls through the screens, large impurities such as sticks, straw, string and large pieces of earth are removed. A powerful fan sucks out as muchdust as possible from the hopper while thecoffee falls through the screen. Aspiration is very important in a coffee mill. Aspiration also helps to improve the working environment. Further, as the coffee flows into precleaning and de-stoning section the combined actions of sifting and pneumatic separation helps to remove stones and pebbles etc. The coffee flows over an inclined vibrating table. The table surface is made from wire mesh through which a controlled airstream penetrates, ftom below. This lifis the coffee beans which float downwards on the air current along the sloping table to be discharged over the edge. Heavier materials such as stones, pieces of metal, glass, etc are not lifted bythe air current and are moved by the table’s oscillating motion to the other edge, where they will be discharged. Magnets are also installed in the pre-cleaning section tore move metal particles. An efficient peeler should peel the coffee completely at low temperatures viz., without high pressure and heat; other wise the arabica parchment coffee tends to lose the bean shape and colour. The clean coffee what weget after winnowing is called bulk coffee. vi) Grading In bulk coffee the beans are not uniform in size, shape, density and colour. When such a bulk coffee is roasted it does not produce uniform roast or a clean cup. Therefore, it is essential to separate the coffee beans based on size, shape, density and colour which will enable to carry out a more uniform roast and to prepare a better cup. Grading by size: Primary grading is carried out based on the size of the beans. Grading is done with the help of flat screen graders or drum graders. Grading by shape: The pea berry beans are separated from the flat beans by using PB band separators. Grading by density: Secondary grading is done based on densimetric classification of individual graders. Catadors (pneumatic Central Coffee Research Institul air separators) and gravity separators are used for the densimetric classification of coffee.

heading: SECONDARY PROCESSING OF COFFEE
text: Grading by density: Secondary grading is done based on densimetric classification of individual graders. Catadors (pneumatic Central Coffee Research Institul air separators) and gravity separators are used for the densimetric classification of coffee. The catadors use air to separate beans of different densities. Gravity separators are also used to separate heavy beans and light beans. The choice between installing catadors or gravity separators (or both) depends on the product to be processed and export quality demanded. Ideally best results will be achieved if the coffee is first separated by size, then the main accepted grades should be passed through catadors and only then over a gravity separators. For instance, the ‘baggy/oily’ off-taste arises from the mineral oil used in the manufacture of jute bags in which coffee is stored. heading: COFFEE FARM OPERATIONS
text: As per the recent survey report, the number of labourers required ‘for effectively managing one acre of plantation ts about 0.7 labour per day in arabica, 0.4 labour per day for unirrigated robusta and 0.41 labour per day for irrigated robusta. The cost of labour alone constitutes about 60% to 70% of the total cultivation costs in case of arabica and about 55% to 65% in the case of robusta coffee depending on whether irrigated (or) not. In recent years, shortage of skilled labourers in coffee plantation is acute due to migration of workers to urban areas in search of better living. The old generation workers employed on the farms is retiring due to aging and the non-availability of young workers, especially skilled workers for carrying out certain critical operations like shade lopping, weeding, tracing of white stem borer infested plants, pruning etc., is affecting the coffee plantations seriously. Thus, there is an imperative need to introduce mechanization to the possible extent to carry out farm operations for improving the efficiency & productivity of labour and to reduce the cost of production. The mechanization, though difficult to achieve, remains a viable option to overcome the scarcity of labourers in the plantation sector.

The suggested methods of land modifications and planting designs for different field situations to enable mechanization are as follows: Flat land to gentle slopes Flat lands and gentle sloping lands do not require any land modification or land shaping. In such areas, adopting hedge row method of planting across the slope would be highly desirable. The most commonly adopted spacing for hedge rows is 1.8 m x 0.9 m (6x3 ft.) for arabica coffee. Because of closer spacing of plants within a row, stems of the plants are covered more and thus reduce the chances of white stem borer attack. When planted in hedge rows, it is advised to construct farm paths (about 3 m wide) between 4 and 6 hedge rows for facilitating movement of small tractors or walking behind type of rubberized track carriers etc.

Contour farming is the technique of growing crops ‘on the level’ across or perpendicular to a slope rather than up and down the slope. The rows running across the slope are designed to be as level as possible to facilitate planting operations on the contour, Contour farming is most effective on slopes above 10%. Contour farming is not well suited to rolling topography having a higher slope with maximum irregularity. The contour bunds fortified with earthen embankment can act as narrow farm path for facilitating movement of small tractors or walking behind type rubberized track carriers etc. These farm paths can be fortified by planting soil binding grasses like Vetiver, Paspalum etc., on the lower side. In India, coffee is cultivated using a silvihorticulture approach, where it is grown under the shade of trees to achieve optimal performance. This setup allows various economic species to grow together. The shade created by the trees is perfect for growing different types of fruits, cash crops, and spices alongside coffee. Since the hilly areas with fragmented holdings are not suitable for intensive cultivation of a single crop, it becomes essential to grow multiple crops in coffee farms. The soil and climate in coffee-growing regions, especially in the Western Ghats, are perfect for growing a wide variety of fruits and spices. The key is to choose compatible crops with different canopy and root structures. This way, the crops’ canopies capture sunlight at different heights, and their roots access moisture and nutrients from various depths without affecting the coffee plants’ growth, Intercropping in young coffee: Maximizing revenue and soil health When coffee plants are young and newly planted in cleared areas, farmers can practice intercropping by growing annual Central Coffee Research Institute crops alongside the coffee to generate additional income in the initial years. heading: COFFEE PLANTATIONS
text: When coffee plants are young and newly planted in cleared areas, farmers can practice intercropping by growing annual Central Coffee Research Institute crops alongside the coffee to generate additional income in the initial years. The intercrops may compete with coffee for water and nutrients, so it is crucial to take proper care to ensure that there is enough soil moisture and nutrition available for both the intercrops and the young coffee plants. In the Wayanad region of Kerala, it is common to grow intercrops like ginger and turmeric in rows along with coffee. This helps to enhance soil fertility and overall crop health. Systematic study on diversification of crops in coffee plantations The Coffee Board of India took a significant step in agricultural development by launching a project in 1973 focused on diversifying coffee holdings in the country. The aim was to enhance overall productivity by adopting modern scientific methods, increasing coffee production, and making the farms economically viable through additional crops that could supplement income. Funded by the Diversification Fund of the International Coffee Organization, the project established a diversification farm in Chettalli village, Coorg district, Karnataka, in 1973. Two major experiments were conducted to study the feasibility and economics of cultivating different crops alongside coffee (mixed cropping). The first experiment explored combining coffee with known associate crops like mandarin orange, black pepper, and banana for both arabica and robusta coffee, either individually or in combination with other crops. The second experiment adopted 4 multi-storeyed cropping pattern with strip Central Coffee Research Institul' planting, organizing coffee, shade trees, and associate crops in strips to manage them individually and reduce competition.

Among the specialty coffees, sustainable coffees are emerging as the most important segment due to concerns about protecting the environment, consumer health, and the welfare of small growers and workers. Unlike other specialty coffees, sustainable coffees are characterized by a unique feature: certification of operations from farm to the final retail outlet. Sustainable coffees broadly comprise organic coffee, fair-trade coffee, and shade grown, eco-friendly, or bird friendly coffees. Organic coffees are those produced by management practices that help conserve or enhance soil structure, resilience, and fertility. These practices involve using only non-synthetic nutrients and plant protection methods. Furthermore, while many producers grow coffee without the use of synthetic agrochemicals, this passive approach is not sufficient to be considered organic in the absence of credible certification.

Two factors of paramount importance for farm designing are the diverse topography and available coffee varieties. Bio-fertilizers Bio-fertilizers, strictly speaking, are not fertilizers that directly provide nutrition to crop plants. They consist of cultures of microorganisms like bacteria and fungi, packed in a carrier material. The essential component in Bio-fertilizers is the microorganisms themselves. These microorganisms indirectly aid plants by enhancing Nitrogen (N) fixation or improving nutrient availability in the soil. Bio-fertilizers can be defined as “microbial inoculants that contain live or latent cells of selected strains of nitrogen-fixing, phosphate-solubilizing microorganisms used for application to seed, soil, or composting areas to accelerate certain microbial processes; thereby increasing the availability of nutrients in easily assimilable forms to plants”. Classification and factors affecting the effectiveness of bio-fertilizers Bio-fertilizers can be classified into three classes: Nitrogen-fixing, Phosphorus-mobilizing, and organic matter decomposing. Nitrogen-fixing biofertilizers include Rhizobium, Azotobacter, Azospirillum, Bluegreen Algae, and Azolla. Phosphate solubilizers are Bacillus, Pseudomonas, and Aspergillus niger, while phosphorus Central Coffee Research Institute absorbers are Vesicular Arbuscular Mycorrhizae (VAM) fungi.

Organic matter decomposing biofertilizers are categorized into two major types; Cellulolytic and Lignolytic. The effectiveness of a particular biofertilizer depends on several critical factors. These factors include the suitability of the species of the organism for the target group, the strain’s specificity and suitability for a specific crop, and its compatibility with the existing agro-eco conditions, such as soil pH, moisture, and environmental factors. To ensure effectiveness, it is crucial to maintain aseptic conditions during manufacturing and ensure the proper cell count of living organisms in the carrier material while maintaining purity and minimizing contamination. Additionally, the condition and quality of the carrier material play a role in determining the biofertilizer’s shelf life. Storing biofertilizers separately from chemicals like fertilizers, fungicides, and pesticides in cool places is important to preserve their efficacy.

Pest, disease, and weed management Pests, diseases, and weeds are managed judiciously through proper shade regulations and by adopting integrated management practices involving physical, mechanical, and biological methods. For example, in arabica coffee, stem borer can be effectively controlled by wrapping the stem with non-woven fabric. Coffee berry borer and shot hole borer can be controlled by installing traps in the field and mealybugs can be controlled by releasing parasites. For proper care and maintenance of motor, the following points need to be considered: The voltage available at the motor terminals should be within 10% of the rated voltage of the motor on load The variation of frequency should be limited to 5% above or below the standard frequency The ambient temperature should not exceed 40°C for motor of standard design Motor should be protected from dust, moisture and excessive humidity Drive should be selected carefully. Electric Motor Pump Sets: Quite often it is found that the power supply is faulty and due to which the motors either burn Central Coffee Research Institute or operate under hazardous conditions. Sometimes one of the three phases fails and the motor is burnt. Therefore, the motor has to be properly protected by using any one or all of the following devices and precautions: ¢ Install a voltmeter and check the voltage supply frequently. When the voltage drops below 180, switch off until the voltage comes back to normal ¢ Install an ammeter of a range suitable to your motor. The ammeter gives the amount of electric current in the motor. Every motor carries on its name plate the maximum amperes it withstands under full load conditions.

heading: ESTATE MANAGEMENT
text: When the voltage drops below 180, switch off until the voltage comes back to normal ¢ Install an ammeter of a range suitable to your motor. The ammeter gives the amount of electric current in the motor. Every motor carries on its name plate the maximum amperes it withstands under full load conditions. Hence the amperes recorded on the ammeter should not exceed the figure indicated on the name plate. With the drop in voltage the ampere reading will increase, and running the motor when the ammeter reading is in excess will result in heating and ultimately burn the motor. To a certain extent, the load on the motor can be reduced by adjusting (decreasing) the quantity of water pumped by the pump using a gate valve ¢ Install a single phase preventer and this will positively disconnect the power supply whenever anyone phases fails « A gate valve must be installed on every pump to regulate the water discharge from the pump. heading: 1.1 Preservation of coffee baskets in the nursery
text: Since majority of coffee estates depend entirely on the supply of bamboo baskets for raising basket plants, the durability of these baskets has to be ensured as they are generally attacked by wetrot caused by saprophytic fungi and moulds etc. Copper sulphate is toxic to the moulds and other fungi. Hence a three year study was conducted in the Coffee Experiment Station to determine the economical strength of copper sulphate to be used with advantage. The experiments demonstrate the fact that boiling the baskets in at least 2% copper sulphate solution is essential to confer upon them immunity from the inroads of destructive moulds which cause delay and hasten rotting. Treating the baskets in the above manner has enhanced their lasting quality. The method of treatment is discussed in detail (Srinivasan, 1936).

heading: 1.2 Phytotoxicity of BHC
text: It was reported that the hydrocarbons such as Benzene and Toluene when used in sufficient amounts they became markedly toxic and act as cytolities to disrupt cellular organization. A preliminary study was undertaken to observe the effect of BHC on seedlings and germinating seeds. BHC treated plants showed marked intervenal chlorosis of new leaves. The control plants were normal. There was general stunting of linear growth of plants in BHC treatment. The percentage emergence was poor and recorded only 23%. Instead of normal, buttons of certain seedlings got stuck in the soil while their stubby roots were exposed. On examination various malformations of root were noticed in BHC treatment. Abnormal seedlings when shifted to the bed with normal soil appeared to give fresh roots. heading: 1.4 Polythene bags for raising coffee seedlings
text: The results ofa trial in the nursery to compare the growth of coffee seedlings in polythene bags with those grown in baskets or beds conducted during 1961 and 1963 revealed that seedlings in polythene bags were superior to those grown in baskets or secondary beds in terms of height of the seedlings, number of leaves produced, shoot and root weight. Since the seedlings in polythene bags developed better and balanced shoot and root, they will be able to withstand the transplanting shock better. In addition, they are cheaper by way of initial cost. They do not require any fungicidal treatment before use in the case of baskets. They also conserve more moisture and hence require less frequent watering. Though there was practically no difference in growth of seedlings among the 2 type of bags. black polythene bags appear to withstang weather conditions, wear and tear much bette than white bags, and therefore may be Preferred (Gopalakrishnan, 1964).

heading: 1.8 Studies on hastening of germination of
text: Arabica coffee seed and further growth of seedlings. 1. Hastening of germination Effect of pre-sowing of S.795 Arabica coffee seeds (with parchment) in aqueous solution of 22 different chemicals as also with various water soaking treatment (both under lab and nursery conditions) was studied and was consistently observed that about 50% of the total seeds soaked for 24 hours in Ascorbic acid (0.1%), Folic acid (0.1%) and Thiourea (1500 ppm) germinated earlier by about 5-7 days. The percentage of seed germination was generally better with these chemicals as compared to control seeds (Gopal and Ramaiah, 1971).

heading: 1.9 Studies on the physiology of germination of coffee seed. I. Observations on sprouting
text: Germination of Coffea arabica cultivar S.795 seeds was studied under natural conditions in nursery and laboratory. Seeds without parchment germinated much earlier than those with parchment intact. Possible causes for the delay in germination of seeds with parchment are discussed (Gopal and Ramaiah, 1972).

heading: 1.10 Seed germination in coffee
text: In Arabica 50%, 75% and fully ripened show higher germination than 25% ripened. In Canephora similar trends are seen in counts at 50" day. Observations on 50" and 100" day revealed that covering of beds with polythene chamber either alone or with paddy straw is superior to ordinary bed covered with paddy straw. Covering of sowing beds with polythene sheets likewise indicate higher percentage of germination by 50" day itself and 100° day onwards an increased percentage of germination. The failure of many sceds to germinate may have no relation to a need for pre-treatment but may be due to merely to requirement of specific conditions. Temperature is amongst the most important conditions. Use of chemicals or hormones or tepid water requires further probing with the use of polythene bags (Vishveshwara and Suryakantha Raju, 1972).

heading: 1.11 Effect of placement of seeds on germination
text: TA: Seed with groove downwards (embryo at the top of the surface) Seed with groove upwards (embryo at lower surface) TC: Seed with groove perpendicular to soil surface (embryo at the top of the surface) TD: Seed with groove perpendicular to soil surface (embryo at the bottom of the surface) TB: the Seed with embryo at bottom recorded the lowest value of soldier stage at 41*t day while seed with groove upwards recorded significantly high value over this and other 2 treatments. By 105" day the treatment differences are eliminated. Unfolding of cotyledons and initiation of first pair of leaves is significantly high in TB while these are affected and delayed in TD where loop formation is absent. Present study show that sowing seeds with embryo at the bottom is not conducive to good germination and sowing should be either flat-groove upward or downward or embryo at the top. With the parchment intact it is not possible to know the location of the embryo. Therefore, sowing as in TC embryo at the top is not practicable (Vishveshwara and Suryakantha Raju, 1973).

heading: 1.12 Effect of pesticides on coffee seedlings
text: The present study was undertaken to find out the effect of the commonly used pesticides on young coffee seedlings. When the seedling reached the first pair stage, the root system of each seedling was drenched with 10 ml of the insecticide or the fungicide solution. At the end of 2 months, visual observations on phytotoxicity, measurement of height of seedlings and count of number of leaves were made. There were no phytotoxicity symptoms on the foliage of treated and untreated (control) seedlings. Difference in the height and number of leaves were also not statistically significant. But the weight of root system showed significant difference between the control and treated seedlings. The seedlings in the control plot had heavier root system than all the treated seedlings. It is evident that the above pesticides used for the control of pests and diseases in the nursery had an adverse effect on the development of the young root system possibly by interfering with the mitotic division. Cytological studies did not show any malformations in the tip cells (Venkataramaiah and Deepak Singh, 1976).

heading: 1.13 Studies on the effect of some granular contact insecticides on the roots of coffee seedlings
text: Application of Ekalux 5G and Phendal 5G (up to 5g/bag) and Sevin 4G (up to 25g/bag) does not cause any injury to coffee roots. No toxic symptoms were noticed on the shoots either. Application of BHC in the nursery bags resulted in development of stubby roots and arrested the growth of root system. Therefore, these chemicals can be safely used in nursery for control of soil pests (Chacko et al., 1980).

heading: 1.14 Studies on the effect of pre-soaking treatments on seed germination and seedling growth of Coffea canephora
text: Effect of alternate pre-soaking and drying of C. canephora seeds in ash water solution on germination and seedling growth was studied. Periodical observations were made on_ the germination of the seeds and on the different growth stages of seedling development. The eed pre-soaked in ash water solution alone nd in combination with shade drying recorded igher rates of germination and seedling growth Shivarama et al., 1981). 15. In the stud endosperm and germling and growth of radica hypocotyl and cotyledon leaves were periodical] recorded. Data indicate the importance of resery, foods of endosperm on the initial developmen of embryo into seedling. heading: 1.16 Studies on the effect of Sevidol 4:4 G on roots of coffee seedlings
text: Investigations on the effect of Sevidol 4:4 G (Carbaryl+Linane) on the root system of coffee seedlings were carried out. No deleterious effect, were noticed. Thus, this granular insecticide at the rate of 10 g per seedling could be safely used for the control of root pests like cockchafers (Venkatesuly et al., 1981).

heading: 1.17 Studies on the effect of Nexagan 5G ang
text: Oftanol 5G on roots of coffee seedlings Two new granular insecticides, Nexagan (Bromophos-ethyl) 5 G and Oftanol (Isofenphos) 5G, have given effective control of white grubs in the nursery. A study was conducted to find out if the use of these has any deleterious effect on the roots of coffee seedlings. No phytotoxicity was observed up to the 30" day after the treatment, When the root system was examined after 15 and 30 days, no abnormal growth was noticed. There was little difference in the dry matter percentage of roots between the treated and untreated plants. The present study showed that the insecticides used do not cause any deleterious effect on coffee seedlings (Gokuldas Kumar et al., 1981).

heading: 1.18 Temperature control of physiological dwarfing in coffee seedlings
text: In the present study, endosperm present on the embryo of coffee seed was scraped to expose the embryo. Seeds started germinating within 48 hours. On 7" day these germlings were transplanted to pots. The growth was faster up to opening of ‘Seq 'dy, Cal "Ve “nt of Sal 0) o =- OO DB ¢ cotyledonary leaves and there after slowed down. Observations recorded after 20 months revealed reduction in height of the plant, length of the internode and size of the leaf. They had very poor root system (Purushotham and _ Sreenivasan, 1982).

heading: 1.19 Effect of Lindane 20 EC and BHC 50 WP on coffee seedlings
text: BHC at 0.5% and 1% and Lindane at 0.1% a.i. showed reduction in the dry matter percentage of roots. Lindane at 0.075% a.i. did not show any reduction in dry matter percentage of roots and so it could be used at this concentration for the control of root pests in nursery. Otherwise no visual phytotoxic symptoms were noticed (Vinod Kumar et al., 1983).

heading: 1.20 Seed borne fungi
text: Twenty six fungi representing different genera isolated from the seeds of Arabica. More number of fungi was isolated from the seeds with parchment than those removed of their parchment. Geotrichum candidum and _ Fusarium solani occurred in greater proportion than the other fungi. During seed germination on moist filter paper these fungi infected and killed the embryo and such seeds failed to germinate because of preemergence of rotting of embryo on the nursery beds (Muthappa, 1984).

heading: 1.21 Studies on the seed characters of some coffee species
text: The morphological differences of seed features in 12 species of Coffea available in gene bank were studied. The overlapping of different species in their center of origin perhaps has caused introgressive hybridization between some species of Liberica group resulting in broadening of genetical base that has manifested in this variability. It is possible that Arabica being selfpollinated species, tend to show narrow variation than other species who have predominantly crosspollinating reproductive mechanism. These limits offer good sources for exploitation in breeding programme in coffee and stresses the necessity of prior identification of plants possessing desirable seed features (Jamsheed Ahmed, 1984).

heading: 1.22 Bethel spray to overcome dormancy in coffee seedlings
text: Bethel (2-chloro ethyl phosphoric acid) @ 125, 250, 500 and 1000 ppm was sprayed to break the dormancy of seedlings (SIn.7.3) at button stage. The results showed that the seedlings sprayed with Bethel 250 ppm unfolded their cotyledonary leaves with the increase in plant height and number of leaves as compared to control (Shivarama et al., 1986).

heading: 1.23 Flower induction in juvenile coffee seedlings
text: Flower induction in juvenile coffee seedlings (S.274) was tried with different surgical and growth regulator treatments in pot culture experiment. Gibberlic acid (GA3) sprays were found to be effective in flower bursting while the other growth regulator sprays and surgical treatment like girdling, bark inversion and bending of main stem failed to induce flowering. The influence of each treatment on morphology of seedlings observed has been reported. Gibberlic acid induced flowering within 6 months after the spray, when the seedlings were at the stage of 24 months (Raghuramulu and Purushotham, 1987).

heading: 1.24 Seed germination and seedling growth as influenced by nursery soil mixture
text: Since good jungle soil is not easily accessible in every plantation and in many coffee plantations ordinary estate soils are being used in nursery soil mixture, studies were conducted to find out a suitable composition. Of the various compositions of soil, FYM and sand tried, the mixture of 5:3:1 ratio seemed to be more effective and conducive for early as well as higher seed germination of Robusta. Growth parameters also revealed that 5:3:1 mixture was more suitable for seedling growth (Veerendra Kumar and Raju, 1988).

heading: 1.25 Studies on the phytotoxic effect of systemic granular insecticides on coffee grown in polythene bags
text: Disystron 5G, Rogor 5G, Solvirex 5G and Thimet 10G caused phytotoxicity to coffee grown in polythene bags and that of Temik 10G is safe. No appreciable difference could be noticed in phytotoxic effect of plants in bags and those of sleeves. It is necessary to exercise caution in the use of these insecticides in nursery (Bhat et al., 1988).

heading: 1.26 Effect of pre-storage and mid- storage treatment on the germination of coffee seeds
text: Maximum germination (84%) of 6 month old stored Arabica seeds was obtained by soaking them either in Sodium phosphate (Dibasic) 250 ppm or in EDTA disodium salt for 48 hours before sowing. Cycocel and EDTA soaking treatment (for 24 hours) on freshly prepared Robusta seeds resulted in highest germination (91-97%) after 45 days of seed preparation (Raghuramulu and Purushotham, 1991).

heading: 1.27 Study on the effect of biofertilizers on the growth of CxR coffee seedlings
text: In a nursery study on the effect of different biofertilizers (Nitrogen fixing and Phosphorus mobilizing) on the growth of CxR coffee seedlings, it was observed that Azospirillum brasilense treatment significantly increased the plant height. There was also a significant increase in stem girth, tap root length and total root weight by combined application of Azospirillum brasilense + Phosphobacteria (Bacilus sp.) + VAM fungi (Gigaspora margarita). The results of this experiment indicated that application of biofertilizers could enhance the growth and vigour of CxR coffee seedlings (Glory Swarupa, 1996).

heading: 1.28 Seedling blight - A new disease of coffee seedlings
text: A new disease affecting 18 months old. Coffea arabica cv. Cauvery (Catimor) seedlings was observed for the first time from the Margolly estate, Consolidated Coffee Ltd., Pollibetta. Kodagu Dist., Karnataka during March 1996 caused by the fungus Alternaria alternata is reported here. In the initia] stage of infection a small necrotic spot seen in the nodal region is found to expand later becoming pale brown in colour followed by blightening and drooping of leaves leading to the gradual death of seedlings. 50-60 plants (2%) were affected during the month of March 1996 (Hanumantha et al., 1996).

heading: 1.29 Influence of commercial organic manures on the growth of coffee seedlings
text: A study was carried out at Central Coffee Research Institute for 2 years during 1995-96 with an objective of comparing the effectiveness of three commercial organic sources of coconut coir pith compost viz., Prajwala neem, Varanasi-cocompost-O (VCC-O, 100% organic), Varanasi-cocompost-F (VCC-F, enriched) and a vermicompost prepared at Central Coffee Research Institute using exotic earthworms Eudrilus euginiae with FYM and as a substitute for FYM in standard nursery mixture. These studies indicated that commercial coir pith compost namely Prajwala neem and vermicompost from exotic earthworms E. euginiae are superior to conventional FYM and could be used in preparation of nursery mixture for obtaining vigorous coffee seedlings in nursery (Muralidhara et al., 1996).

heading: 1.30 Effect of biofertilizers on germination of coffee seed
text: The studies conducted on the efficacy of seed treatment of coffee seeds with biofertilizers on percentage germination indicated that seed treatment with Phosphobacteria (at 10g/100 seeds) a day prior to sowing enhanced the germination compared to other treatments such as ash, Azospirillum, VAM, Azospirillum + Phosphobacteria, Azospirillum + WAM and Azospirillum + Phosphobacteria + VAM (Glory Swarupa et al., 1997).

heading: 2.2.17 Male sterility in Coffea liberica
text: A study of floral characters of the four male sterile plants indicated that the flowers were several times smaller than the normal hermaphrodite flowers. heading: 2.2.31 Physical characteristics of coffee beans as selection indices
text: Indian coffee is known world over for its quality. The planter is paid based on the visual assessment of his produce. Further, extra remuneration is based on the cup quality. The produce is graded into Peaberry and A, B, C and T grades based on the physical standards of measurement and appearance. At Central Coffee Research Institute, breeding is in progress since its inception. In the breeding programme importance is given for maximizing the production of A’ grade beans by eliminating the triage components. So far 12 Arabica and three Robusta genotypes have been released for commercial cultivation. In this article, procedures adopted to obtain the superior bean characteristics for commercial acceptance are discussed (Sreenivasan, 1988).

heading: 2.2.32 A study of pea berry development- its implications in coffee breeding
text: Peaberry development in the parents and progenies of Devamachy hybrids (SIn.5) of coffee has been studied. Empty locule formation is found to be due to the post fertilization abnormalities. A breeding scheme to evolve lines with reduced pea berry and empty locule production is suggested on the basis of data presented. This involves the selection of individual plants with low pea berry production and high self-compatibility from the F,, progeny and further testing for fertility and adaptability (Santa Ram et al., 1990).

heading: 2.2.35 Interspecific hybrid sterility in coffee
text: Various factors acting as barriers of reproduction among the sister plants of F, progenies of 6 interspecific hybrids involving 6 diploid species of the genus Coffea were studied. The osmotic concentration of the protoplasm of the pollen and stigmatic tissue and the reduced genetic variability of the hybrid population with regard to self-sterility alleles were proposed to be the possible barriers of reproduction and thus the cause of sterility in these hybrids. The possible model for increasing the productivity in these hybrids: F,’s of totally compatible parents would be exploited. A number of biparental F,, hybrids should be raised to have a large pool of self-sterility alleles. Natural crossing of these hybrids can be brought about by planting them in alternate rows (Santa Ram et al., 1992).

While differences among hybrids from three parental cross groups were not significant, seasonal variations were highly significant, especially for fruit floats and yield. The Tall x Tall crosses showed the highest heritability and genetic advance, while Dwarf x Tall hybrids produced more fruits per cluster. Progenies from Cauvery x S.881 (Rume Sudan Wild Arabica) and interspecific C. arabica (Cauvery) x C. canephora (CxR) crosses exhibited lower fruit weight and volume, likely due to robusta genome integration (Anil Kumar et al., 2013).

heading: 2.2.40 Monohybrid Mendelian segregation in an interspecific hybrid population of tetraploid x diploid Coffea species- part 2
text: Coffee exhibits normal sexual propagation with significant variation, though its extent remains poorly understood. A study (2008-2011) at Coffee Research Sub Station, Chettalli, analyzed monohybrid segregation in the F, population of C. arabica cv. ‘Cauvery’ x (C. congensis x C. canephora var. robusta). The results showed that dependent and independent traits varied in expression, with independent traits following Mendelian segregation (3:1 and 1:2:1 ratios) at high confidence levels (P > 0.50 to 0.95). Dominant traits included dwarf bush, thin stem, and short primary branches, while tall bush, thick stem, and longer branches were recessive (Anil Kumar et al., 2014).

heading: 3.1.1 Balehonnur coffee selections
text: Breeding of coffee resistant to leaf disease with vigorous growth and fairly average to high yielding qualities commenced in the year 1962. A survey was conducted in all the coffee areas in South India and 267 plants from different zones was thus tapped and nearly.25,000 seedlings were raised. From these 80 mother plants that showed the desirable characters were selected in the first instance and were given serial numbers. At the same time self bred progeny of these mother plants as well as cross-breeds between these and the Kents and Coorgs were also raised. The procedure was continued until in the later generations the leaf disease susceptible segregates were either reduced to the minimum or altogether eliminated. By the year 1938, three mother plants had been finally fixed for further propagation. They are S.26, S.31 and S.44 whose progeny are known as the S.288 family including S.795 and S.333 family including S.645. It is gratifying to note that the performance of these selections in the field under different soil micro-climatic conditions has not belied the expectations. The majority of these selections are both disease resistant, good yielders and of vigorous growth (Narayanan, 1954).

heading: 3.1.2 Station selections
text: An attempt was made in 1949 in order to evaluate the relative yield of the selections (S.446 Kents, S.795, S.645 and S.288) in a manner, which would satisfy the eye of a statistician. Five harvest figures are recorded for 20 single plant selections, which are 100% resistant to leaf disease. If these plant selections continue to maintain their rank and do make good in other characters like bean z size, lower percentage of triage and quality in the cup, it would open up a new vista for the Indian coffee planter (Thomas, 1960).

heading: 3.1.3 Correlation studies in coffee selections.
text: I. Preliminary studies on correlation between stem girth and ripe cherry yield in some coffee selections The present write up relates to the correlation found between stem girth and ripe cherry yield of some Arabica and Robusta selections. The results showed that stem girth has a positive and significant correlation with mean cherry yield in 6 out of the 10 Robusta selections studied while one selection of the ‘t’ test value just fails to attain the 5% level of P. Both selections S.947 and S.948 show a highly significant positive correlation. The coefficient of variation for yield and stem girth is comparatively low in both these selections. This is probably attributable to the selections being advanced generation in straight line selection. This study however indicate that stem girth might be a useful character for purposes of selecting high yielding lines (Srinivasan, 1969).

Selection pressures being adopted in seed plots of these selections maintained in various zones are enumerated (Srinivasan and Vishveshwara, 1980).

heading: 3.1.9 A chemotaxonomic study of some species of Coffea

C. wightiana Wall., and C. travencorensis W. et Arn. was studied by simple chemical tests. The reaction patterns indicate that the varieties and species are chemically distinct and the individual sub-sections of the genus Coffea: Erythrocoffea, Mazambicoffea, Pachycoffea and Paracoffea (Section/Genus) are relatively homogeneous in their chemical constitution. This study also suggests that Erythrocoffea and Pachycoffea are the oldest sub-sections of Eucoffea while Melanocoffea and Mozambicoffea are relatively recent evolutionarily. Paracoffea appears to be a very recent group. The possibility of elevating this gigantic genus to the family status is considered and rejected (Santa Ram, 1983).

heading: 3.1.21 Yield response of some new Arabica coffee selections to Bordeaux spray

From the results it may be said that although leaf rust is not a major problem in these selections, dhe profitability of Bordeaux is seen which can be taken advantage in 5 selections out of 9 evaluated, at the existing level of expenditure of spraying. heading: 3.1.22 Discriminating coffee varieties for early vigour and yield potential in North-East
text: Three year old plants in 8 selections of C. arabica and 6 of C. canephora were studied with reference to 7 morphological characters related to vegetative and reproductive vigour. A comparison of the varieties for percentage increase in growth, maximum increase in case of SIn.6 and old Robusta denoting faster growth rate in 2 varieties. However, the average percentage increase was more in Robusta than Arabica. Out of 8 discriminate functions fitted to the data, the one having 4 characters namely plant height, number of primaries, stem girth and flowers/node was found to give maximum discrimination indicating greater importance and reliability of these characters for selection for improvement of yield in coffee. heading: 3.1.23 Growth performance of some coffee selections in Andhra Pradesh

Nagar, Andhra Pradesh. The’ characters, number of primaries, number of nodes per primary, length of primary, brush spread and plant height show significant variation among the selections. Selection 7 produced maximum number of primaries and number of nodes per primary. Because of its dwarf and compact nature, the plant showed least height, length of primary and bush spread. Of the remaining selections, the order of performance is SIn. 5, 6, 3 and 8 respectively. Stem girth, bush spread, number of nodes per primary and yield per plant showed significant variations among the years during which they were studied (Santa Ram et al., 1992).

heading: 3.1.24 Performance of 5 Arabica Coffee selections in Karnataka and Tamil Nadu
text: Zone A survey was undertaken to assess the performance of 5 Arabica coffee cultivars viz., S.795, SIn.5, Sln.6, Sln.8, SIn.7 and Sln.9 in different agro-climatic zones of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. The survey showed varied performance of different cultivars in various zones. In Chikkamagaluru zone, S.795, SIn.5 (S.2931) and Sln.9 were the top performers compared to other selections whereas, in Aldur/Mudigere. Sakleshpur/Somwarpet and Coorg zones, SIn.5, 6 and 8 showed better performance. In Pulneys (Tamil Nadu). Sln.5, 6 and 9 were the best performers. In Shevaroys, S.795 and Sln.9 averaged higher than others. Considering the performance overall the zones, SIn.8 and S.795 indicated better yield responses to favorable environment while, Sln.5 showed marginal response. The differential performance of the cultivars is attributed to interaction between their genetic compliments and the environment (Jamsheed Ahmed et al., 1995).

heading: 3.5.3 Optimum plot size for field trials with

Cauvery; namely S. 4345 and S. 4347. The CV was calculated for plot sizes from 1 to 60 trees, arranged in plots of rows or columns. The Fairfield Smith equation (y= a x xt) and the generalized law (y = a x re! x c®) were fitted to the data for plot size (x), comprising rows (r) and columns (c), CV (y) and heterogeneity coefficient (g).
