heading: 4.1 Studies on polyploids of Coffea
text: The basic chromosome number of the genus Coffea is 11. The effects of ploidy on the organisms are varied. Though gigantism is a common feature in the higher ranges of ploidy, it is however, not a universal phenomenon. Observations recorded indicated the pentaploid and octoploid studied show a higher number of stomata than expected. Individuals in any particular population appear to show variation with regard to number of stomata. The stomatal number in the tetraploid’ plants of cultivar Kents and in S.288 ranges from 133.88 to 188.71/ sq.mm. The size of aperture is not correlated with chromosome number. From the present studies it may be concluded that in general the number of stomata in the leaf decreases from diploid to octoploid in coffee (Achyuta and Vishveshwara, 1960).

heading: 4.2 Occurrence of a haploid in Coffea arabica
text: During December 1959 two branches on the haploid were found with big sized leaves. An experimentation of shoot tip from these showed adjacent cells with 22 and 44 chromosomes. The leaves on these branches are broader, thicker and crinkled. This appears to be a case of spontaneous chromosome doubling and such phenomenon has been recorded in other crops like maize also (Vishveshwara, 1960).

heading: 4.3 A preliminary report on meioticirregularities in diploids and diploid interspecific hybrids in coffee
text: Studies on meiosis in F,, of Coffea excelsa x C. eugenioides and C. liberica x C. eugenioides and the parent plants are presented in the paper. 39 - ens ey Parent plant in C. liberica is highly regular. Plants in F,, show irregularitics such as failure of pairing, unequal distribution of chromosomes chromatin bridges and precocious cytokinesis whereas the parent plants in C. excelsa and C. eugenioides show only chromatin bridges occasionally. The irregularities in F, are considered as the probable cause for the gametic sterility and sterility in fruitset. The formation of chromatin bridges in the parent plants of two diploid species indicate that detailed studies of these and other species-in the genus Coffea are important and may throw more light on the full significance of this phenomenon (Vishveshwara, 1963).

heading: 4.4 Induced auto-tetraploid in Coffea canephora
text: Pierre Ex Froehner The technique employed to induce tetraploidy in the shoot portion of seedlings and the subsequent growth of these gigas characters and flowering showed the success of the colchicine used technique. The colchicine induced auto-tetraploid in Coffea canephora (2n=22) showed the highest association of chromosomes was quadrivalents. Bivalents are considerably more and univalents and trivalents are fewer. Meiotic irregularities are also very few. The sterility of the induced auto-tetraploid is attributed to meiotic, genetic and physiological imbalances. However, self incompatibility is maintained at the tetraploid level as there was no fruit set on selfing (Vishveshwara and Chinnappa, 1965).

heading: 4.7 Effect of maleic hydrazide on meiosis in coffee
text: In the present experiment it is seen that in case of Coffea canephora the divisions started 24 hours after placing the cut twigs in distilled water, while in case of Coffea arabica it was after 46 hours. Different concentrations of Maleic hydrazide have effected delay in the commencement and have also prolonged the duration of meiotic divisions. At higher concentration from 5000 ppm both delay in commencement as well as prolonged duration of meiosis were more prominent. It is interesting to note that Maleic hydrazide at a concentration of 10000 ppm had no adverse effect on the divisions except that the duration was more i.e., 8 hours in Cc. canephora and 10 hours in C. arabica as against the control 4 hours and 5 hours respectively. C. canephora seems to be affected more than C. arabica. From this it is quite evident that the chemicals also act as a meiotic depressors in coffee (Chinnappa, 1968).

heading: 4.8 Observations on the effect of moisture on microsporogenesis in coffee
text: Coffee is known to blossom after pre- blossom rains. Irrigation also induces blossom. However blossom is also induced when twigs with welldeveloped flower-buds are cut and kept in moist chambers. This indicates that surface absorption of adequate moisture induces flower opening. Several factors like plant condition, its foliage, flower bud size, drought and quantity of water are known to influence blossom. In the present study observations on the effect of moisture on meiosis under different atmospheric temperature and humidity conditions are presented. After the receipt of water microsporogenesis leading to pollen formation and megasporogenesis leading to the organization of the embryo-sac are initiated. Atmospheric humidity seems to influence the rapidity of meiotic divisions both in C. arabica as ee CYTOLOGY and C. canephora. The initiation and duration of meiotic divisions are earlier and shorter in C. canephara. Factors affecting the blossom are discussed (Chinnappa, 1969).

heading: 4.9 Octoploidy in Coffea arabica
text: Morphology and cytology of three octoploid forms of Coffea arabica were studied. A comparison of the morphological characters of natural allotetraploids and the derived octoploids indicates that there is a reduction in size from tetraploidy to octoploidy. The inferiority in vegetative vigour and high sterility of the octoploids suggests that the optimum chromosome number has been reached in nature at the tetraploid level. Occurrence of a high frequency of quadrivalents in meiosis of the octoploids presently studied is contrary to the reports of earlier workers where quadrivalents were not observed. The significance of quadrivalent formation is discussed (Chinnappa, 1969).

heading: 4.10 Interspecific hybrids of Coffea canephora and C. liberica
text: Plant morphology and metaphase 1 chromosome association of six hybrids between C. canephora (subsection Erythrocoffea of section Eucoffea) and C. liberica (subsection Pachycoffea of section Eucoffea) are described. Between plants, variation in the expression of parental characters was observed and attributed to heterozygosity especially in the liberica parent. Bivalent frequency was high, but comparable to that of earlier reports. Trivalents and quadrivalents, indicating structural hybridity, were observed here for the first time in such hybrids. In spite of their classification in different subsections and apparent hybridization barrier, the two species have considerable chromosomal homology (Chinnappa, 1970).

heading: 4.12 Dormancy break and meiotic division in flower buds of Liberica coffee
text: In C. liberica the mature flower buds of the size of 10-13 mm containing fully formed PMCs remained dormant till they were exposed to rain. Once exposed to rain, meiosis was initiated in the PMCs at 40 and % h after rain and was found to be completed by 48 h. i.e., within 8 and % hours. The tetrads were however found to persist until at least 16 h. after completion of meiosis. Water and possibly temperature have an effective role on dormancy break, initiation and progress of meiosis. The diploid C. liberica 2n=22 formed eleven regular bivalents at diakinesis and at metaphase I. Further the accompanying stages of meiosis were regular giving rise to four daughter nuclei at the end of telophase II. Various phases of meiosis from prediakinesis to tetrad formation are illustrated in the photomicrographs (Reddy and Narayan, 1974).

heading: 4.13 B chromosomes in C. arabica

This is the first report of the occurrence of such B chromosomes in the genus. It is likely that they are the by-products of structural rearrangements and chromosomal instability associated with hybridity in this tetraploid species (Chinnappa, 1974).

heading: 4.18 A trisomic Coffea canephora
text: The cytology of a trisomic in C. canephora is reported. The plant has several morphological differences from normal C. canephora. Cytology of the plant indicated the presence of an extra chromosome 2n + 1 = 23 which is a trisomic form. Meiosis was regular in the plant with occasional laggards at anaphase I. In the cross C. dewevrei ‘excelsd X C. eugenioides several maternal types occurred, attributed to parthenogenesis. text: Erythrocoffea Developmental characters of anther and male gametophyte in Arabica and Canephora are described and their evolutionary significance is discussed. Cyto-chemical aspects of pollen development are brought out_in detail and their evolutionary and physiological significance is elucidated. A primitive evolutionary status is suggested for these taxa on the basis of this study (Santa Ram et al., 1987).

heading: 4.30 A trisomic Coffea arabica
text: Cytological behaviour and morphological characters ofa trisomic of C..arabica were described. Importance of this trisomic in gene mapping, on the basis of cytological behaviour was indicated. Origin of the trisomic was proposed to be due to the union of a normal gamete and a gamete with extra chromosome derived through non-disjunction of a chromosome pair (Sreenivasan and Santa Ram, 1985).

heading: 4.31 Cyto-chemistry of pollen development in
text: Paracoffea Cyto-chemical aspects of pollen development in a few species of the selection Paracoffea of the genus Coffea L. were out in detail. Anther development in these species confirms to the basic type. Tapetum is secretory. Endothecium completely surrounds the anther locule. Meiosis and simultaneous cytokinesis in the microscope mother cell give rise to tetrahedral, isobilateral and decussate pollen tetrads. Coupled with these primitive ontogenetic features is the presence of starch less pollen in C. travencorensis indicating a relatively advanced evolutionary status of carbohydrates, proteins, lipids and nucleic acids provided a preliminary insight into the developmental physiology of pollen (Santa Ram et al., 1991).

heading: 4.32 Relationship of stomatal length and frequency to ploidy level in coffee
text: There was a positive correlation between stomatal length and ploidy level but expected increase was not observed at triploid and octoploid level and no overlapping occurred among different ploidies. The frequency of stomata could be used as an indirect ploidy indicator. Since stomatal density has been reported to be influenced by environmental factors, consideration of the number of stomatal chloroplasts as an additional parameter is likely to enhance the reliability of the method (Mishra et al., 1991). 4,33. Evaluation of some indicators in Coffea L. indirect ploidy Several indirect ploidy indicators viz., stomatal plastid number, stomatal length, stomatal frequency, leaf area and pollen grain diameter were evaluated for their usefulness in coffee. A positive correlation is observed between the ploidy level and the characters studied except for stomatal frequency, which is negatively correlated. The stomatal plastid number and stomatal frequency were found the most suitable characters as they manifested regular and distinct differences in relation to ploidy level. They can therefore be recommended to screen coffee populations for ploidy at any stage of plant growth (Sreenivasan et al., 1992). i! ec eer aay

heading: 4.34 Ploidylevelitsinfluenceonleaf anatomical features of coffee
text: In general, there were no differences in basic structure of the leaf lamina at different ploidy levels. Increase in ploidy status was associated with the increase in thickness of lamina, epidermis, palisade tissue, spongy tissue and diameter of spongy cells and the relationship observed is discussed in detail. The study in general supports the common concept of regular correlation between the ploidy status and various characters of the plant including the anatomical ones and could be attributed to the different levels of gene dosage in ploidy variants ’ (Prakash et al., 1993).

heading: 4.35 Cytomorphological studies of two polyploid forms of Coffea arabica L.
text: Cytomorphological features of two spontaneous polyploid plants of Coffea arabica var. Cauvery/Catimor have been studied. Morphologically the plants exhibited reduced phenotype and there were marked differences with respect to stomatal features and pollen characteristics in comparison to their tetraploid counterparts. Meiosis was irregular due to asynaptic behaviour of the constituent genomes resulting in high sterility. The polyploids manifested field resistance to leaf rust disease. The differences observed among the ploidy variants could be attributed to the nature of expressing of genes at different levels of genetic make up (Prakash et al., 1993).

Genetic relations were studied among seventeen Coffea arabica selections of Indian and exotic origin using Mahalanobi’s D” statistic involving 11 morphological characters. The selection could be grouped into five clusters with cluster I consisting of nine varieties, cluster II with three varieties, cluster III and IV with two varieties each and cluster V with single variety. heading: 6.1 Studies on morphology and anatomy of certain abnormal growth in Arabica coffee
text: Considerable variation is noticed with regard to these abnormalities in an affected patch. Shoot growth resumed after blossom showers on such affected twigs showed usually a combination of following features in morphology and anatomy. Growth especially continuing on the short internodal terminals was vigorous, stout and very succulent. When the terminal growth ceased, multiple buds became active or fasciation developed in few cases. Leaves were either extra ordinarily fresh, long and broad or longer than broad or small and brittle. Sometime showed cupping inward. Shape of some of the leaves entirely altered. Yellowing and browning of terminal shoot leaves necrosis and premature defoliation. Internally endocarp and developing endosperm showed discoloration. Vegetative growth produced at the end of the South-West monsoon and till October did not show any high degree of abnormalities. On yellow leaves sporulation was meagre and on green leaves leaf rust sporulation was profuse. Symptoms in morphology and anatomy described earlier became more pronounced on bushes that suffered defoliation/defoliation and die-back. It can perhaps be concluded that functional and physiological disorders play a major role in bringing about these abnormalities (Vishveshwara, 1960).

heading: 6.2 Male sterility in coffee.
text: In some varieties of C. arabica like polysperma and anomala, deviations in floral characters are reported to be associated with certain types of growth and vegetative characters and are said to be controlled by single pair of genes with pleiotropic effects. In the present study however, the data are meagre and it is difficult to estimate the pattern Poa 51 ne anes Were ams - oy of inheritance. Morphological studies showed a gradation in the abnormal type. Here opening ix retarded and at times flowers do not respond even to heavy rains. Extreme cases with petaloid anthers and abnormal pistils show poor set and produce highly abnormal seeds and are therefore, commercially undesirable. Most of the plants with abnormal flowers showed very vigorous growth and comparative freedom from leaf disease in field. Male sterile types have been usefully employed in several crops in hybrid seed production. However, use of male sterility for this purpose requires a thorough knowledge of combining ability and inheritance of. sterile and restorer genes (Vishveshwara, 1967).

heading: 6.6 Aerial roots in Coffea canephora
text: Aerial roots were observed hanging in clusters from the apex of the main stem ina 41- year old C. canephora Pierre, plant in the estate of the Central Coffee Research Institute. These roots were seen at about 136 cm from the ground level where there was no chance of getting either soil or any other favorable medium to induce root formation. This was an unusual phenomenon not recorded so far. Attempts were made to induce rooting at the apex of the main stem and side branches in the same plant at the same height by making injury and then covering the injured portion with soil and moss. heading: 6.8 A mutant for pericarp colour in C. canephora leaf sh
text: The present note records the first case of changes in pericarp colour from fruit set to ripening. The plant with the unusual type of pericarp was noticed at Central Coffee Research Institute. It is similar in all taxonomic characters to C. canephora excepting for pericarp colour. The colour of the developing fruit skin was studied from the pepper stage to fully ripened berry using Munsell colour charts for plant tissue. The colour of the pericarp gradually underwent the following changes: from red red-yellow 3/6 to red 4/6 to red yellow-red 6/6 to yellow 7/4 to yellowish green yellow 7/6 to red 5/10, whereas in normal plants the pericarp colour just changed from green to red. Cytological studies revealed that the plant is diploid (2n=22) (Sreenivasan et al., 1980).

heading: 6.9 Aerial roots in Coffee
text: This phenomenon of occurrence of accessory buds (adventitious buds) changing their potential was noticed in four plants in a plot planted in 1932 to Coffea canephora Pierre ex Froehner, and in one plant of S. 905 (C. arabica Linnaeus cv. Kents x S.274 robusta) at the Central Coffee Research Institute. The roots were seen scattered or in lumps on the main trunk and main branches (Fig. 1). The plants were in healthy condition with normal bearing as others in the same plot. The diameter of the trunk was about 42 cm while that of branches averaged 6.5cm. Some of the roots showed a maximum growth of 3.0 cm. Death of root tip due to necrosis was seen in most of the roots. The fourth plant had innumerable roots, but only at 220 cm from ground level. The high humidity prevailing during monsoon period appears to have favoured such adventitious root formation. This phenomenon is not noticed in pure Arabica coffee and it is possible that there is an inherent tendency in Robusta for such behaviour (Purushotham, 1981).

heading: 6.10 A chlorophyll deficient mutant in coffee
text: The present note deals about a spontaneous bud mutation spotted on one plant on F, of C. congensis x C. canephora. The self sheltered leaves were yellowish green in colour. The flower bud number at the nodes of the mutant sucker was significantly lower than that of the normal branches. The chlorophyll contents of normal, pale yellowish green and white leaves were 1.23, 0.39 and 0.00 mg/g respectively. It is inferred that the mutation is located within the chloroplasts and that the normal plastids are left in the midrib portion of the leaf by a rapid sorting mechanism. Further, the efficiency of this sorting mechanism seems to be restricted to the leaf blade alone since the stem remains green throughout the growth period. Development of pale yellowish green colour in the leaves in shade indicates the light sensitivity of this mutant (Santa Ram and Sreenivasan, 1982).

heading: 6.11 Effect of chemical mutagens of coffee
text: Three mutagenic chemicals viz., Diehtyl sulphate (DES), Dimethyl sulphate (DMS) and Ethyl methane sulphonate (EMS) were tried on coffee using 3 cultivars in C. arabica and one in C. canephora. Concentrations used were 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5% aqueous solution on dormant and activated seeds for 24, 28 and 72 hours duration. In all the treatments, percentage of seed germination was reduced and abnormalities in growth of seedlings were noticed. The chemical action was severe on activated seeds. In C. canephora seedling a % 6 Te ony abnormalities were not noticed but percentage germination was reduced. All the varieties had shown good response to mutagenic chemicals. Increased duration of treatment reduced the fermination percentage in many cases. The favorable concentration of chemical appeared to be at 50% L.D. (Sreenivasan and Vishveshwara, 1982).

heading: 6.12 Acrial roots in C. arabica
text: Acrial roots were observed on the main stem of a 48 year old C. arabica cv. Kents. This is an unusual phenomenon in Arabica not recorded so far. The roots were seen at about 96 cm above the ground level. Maximum length was 2.5 cm. Root tips were dry due to the temperature. The high humidity prevailing during the monsoon appeared favorable for formation of such adventitious roots. The accessory buds can alter their potentiality in Arabica in some environments (Zwingly Premkumar, 1982).

heading: 6.19 Petaloidy - A floral abnormality in Arabica coffee
text: Flower abnormalities such as star flowering occurring due to some external and internal factors are found to effect the normal fruit set and thereby reduce the yields. Some plants in older selections of Arabica were found to show the incidence of petaloidy in which the stamen is transferred into petal like structures. Fruit set and retention was found to be quite low under this condition. In the present article, the distinct morphological features of petaloid flowers are described and their influence on fruit set and retention is reported. From the results it could be seen that petaloidy would greatly affect the coffee yields. Normal vegetative growth is seen in these plants. Possible conclusion seems to be these plants may be genetically predisposed to this abnormality (Raghuramulu and Sreenivasan, 1988).

heading: 7.8 Indian coffee (Coffea arabica L.) cultivars and their adaptive significance
text: Leaf architecture including venation pattern was studied in ten different Indian arabica (Coffea arabica L.) cultivars. The leaf size, areole size, number of vein endings entering the areole and vein islets termination number showed variation in different cultivars and is attributed to their origin involving different parents and selection pressure. The adaptive significance of leaf architecture is discussed. The study further indicated that the cultivars, Sln.7.3, SIn.9, SIn.11 and Sin.5 have inherent structural advantage over other arabica cultivars to cope with the water distribution during stress conditions (Mishra et al., 2010).

heading: 7.9 Evaluation of coffee varieties derived from diverse genetic sources of resistance for prospective exploitation - An International cooperative effort
text: Coffee leaf rust (CLR) caused by the obligate parasitic fungus Hemileia vastatrix Berk & Br. and Coffee berry disease (CBD) caused by Colletotrichum kahawe are the two most important diseases of coffee (Coffea arabica L.) causing considerable economic damage. In order to address the problem of CLR and CBD, there is an urgent need to focus research efforts on searching for new sources of resistance, exploitation of the available genetic resources for development of new varieties and to provide resistant and resilient coffee cultivars to farmers. It is imperative to test the potential varieties under realistic conditions to assess their performance (Prakash et al., 2010).

heading: 7.10 Morphological proportions for detection of genetic inheritance in F, progenies of arabica (Coffea arabica L.)
text: Plant architecture is composed of several morphological components combined in a certain proportion to produce the phenotype of the particular species. Consequent to the breeding protocols, this proportion changes from one generation to the other and the offspring possess a new proportion dissimilar to their parents. To identify the genetic traits transmitted by the parents, an attempt was made to measure the morphological ratios between the various components of the F, progenies of dwarf and tall coffee cultivars. The ratios between the changeable characters and within non-changeable characters were separately calculated in the hybrids and the parents and compared (Anil Kumar et al., 2012). 7.11 Screening of Coffea arabica germplasm for Caffeine level A total of 76 collections of coffee bean (Coffea arabica) are being maintained in the germplasm bank at Coffee Research Sub Station in North Kodagu, Karnataka, India. Following evaluation of caffeine level in 34 collections, a wide variability ranging from 1.18% (Misan Taferikala) to 2.07% (Sumatra) with an overall mean value of 1.84%, was observed (Gopinandhan et al., 2015).

Clonal progeny trials had lower levels of variations for individual plant yield than seedling progeny trial and the variation was further reduced when plots of three plants available in the clonal progeny trails considered. heading: 8.1.3 Vegetative propagation in coffee
text: Clonal versus seedling performance in Robusta coffee: An evaluation of morphological characters related to yield 8.1.5. Seventeen clonal and 12 seedling progenies in Robusta coffee (Coffea canephora) were evaluated for five morphological characters related to yield. Clonal progenies showed higher means and lower coefficients of variation compared to seedling progenies for most of the characters. Number of primaries was the most variable character in both kinds of progenies. Heritability estimates were higher in clonal trial I compared to clonal trial II and seedling trial for all the characters, presumably because of the better stand of plants in this trial. Mean yield per se showed higher heritability than any of the characters studied. Stem girth, mean diameter of primaries and bush radius were significantly correlated with mean yield of progénies. Path analysis revealed that stem girth and mean diameter of primaries and leaf size exerted high direct effects on mean yield (Subbalakshmi et al., 1981).

heading: 8.3. MALLET CUTTINGS
text: Mallet cuttings - A new method of vegetative propagation in coffee 8.3.1. Orthotropic shoots of 45-60 days old could be used as mallet cuttings successfully in coffee and thereby the loss of food reserves from mother plant minimized. The low per cent of rooting success could be attributed to the dry conditions prevailing during the period of study. In contrast, a success rate of 85-100% has been reported in monsoon season (June-August) (Anil Kumar and Mir Azizuddin, 1991).

heading: 8.3.2 Response of different growth regulators on rooting of mallet cuttings in coffee

Result showed 90% rooting in IBA, 80% in Planofix and 70% in Alar at 100 ppm concentration level. Highest number of primary and secondary roots were obtained with lowest concentration of IBA (1000 ppm). Control cuttings showed lowest rooting of 30% (Anil Kumar and Srinivasan, 1993).

text: The results of the trial have proved that three substances, Auxins, Carbohydrate and Nitrate in combination are capable of inducing greater root production and earliness in rooting. Deficiency of one or more of these would appear to have been the cause for the varying success obtained in rooting in the earlier trials. Standing the basal ends of the cuttings first in a mixture of 0.2% Ammonium nitrate and 3% Dextrose for 12 hours and then in a solution of B-Indolyl acetic acid at 100g/L for a similar period gave the best results. Response of the more woody fourth internode was comparatively less. Hence it is desirable to collect sucker growths when four internodes are formed, as many further growth is bound to produce in the lowest internode refractory material not suited for quick vegetative propagation (Sundaram, 1953).

heading: 8.4.2 Root suckers in coffee
text: Occurrence of typical cases of suckers from roots in Coffea canephora, Coffea excelsa and Coffea liberica have been noticed in Central Coffee Research Institute and on some private estates. Canephora, excelsa and liberica generally showed typical orthotropic types of suckers all along the thick roots and horizontal or gourmondizer type at the cut end of the root either exposed or submerged in soil. While horizontal or gourmondizer type of suckers were observed all along the thick roots in a few plants in canephora collection s from Ceylon (CCRI No. 240). Orthotropic suckers showed vigorous growth. They formed secondary and tertiary branches with flowers and fruits similar to water sprouts. Formation of new roots was seen at the point of sucker sprouting in case of canephora and excelsa. The horizontal suckers in canephora (CCRI 240) were less vigour and were more than one per point (Suryakantha Raju, 1971).

heading: 8.4.8 Propagation of Robusta coffee through sucker slips
text: When single nodal cuttings are vertically divided into two equal parts, these could give rise to sucker slips. To find out the rooting ability of sucker slips under Indian climatic conditions this study was taken up. A rooting success of 73% with an average number of 2.2 primary roots and 39.1 secondary roots was recorded. Slow shoot growth on the rooted slips was observed. But the shoots were stick and sturdy with short internodes. This method offers the possibilities of producing more number of true to type plants from a limited source of high performing superior clones of Robusta (Anil Kumar, 1994).

heading: 8.5. STUMP PLANTING
text: 8.5.1.A preliminary report on stump planting of Arabica coffee The technique of stump planting can be employed with advantage for utilizing the plant material thinned out from close planted areas. The older stumps with well developed root system planted deep into the soil, on establishment, may withstand severe drought conditions better than seedlings. It is expected that this sturdy and extensive root-system with negligible crown to support may be in a position to tolerate the attack of usual eelworms, so that establishment of G arabica in such eelworm infested areas may not be so difficult as is the case with seedlings. An attempt was made to uproot these stumped plants with as much root system and average suckers as possible. 92% of the stumps have successfully established and no symptoms of water deficit were noticed in any of the standing suckers, which were on stump. The leaves were dark green and healthy. Significant flush activity was noticed. Bud advancement and stray blossom were also noticed (Ananth, 1963).

heading: 8.7.5 Rejuvenation of old coffee with newe selections by cleft grafting A preliminary report
text: Unproductive and moribund coffee, either of Arabica or Robusta could be rejuvenated into newer lines like Cauvery and CxR hybrids by adopting wedge-cleft method of grafting. Uniformity of the population is achieved by this method. Grafting advances blossom and bearing. Cauvery on old Robusta produced better shoot growth than that on San Ramon. The stock scion establishment was highest in Cauvery/San Ramon and it was 88% in CxR on old Robusta. The wood of both the stoa and scion should be in the unlignified cota The graft union was completed in 60 days in he, bow Robusta, 50 days in Cauvery/San Ramon and it was 60-80 days in Cauvery/Robusta. heading: 8.7.6 Top working of C. canephora cv. §.274 with
text: C. arabica cv. Cauvery 72% of the scions survived of the 100 plants grafted. The graft union was completed in 45-60 days. The Cauvery scion began to yield in the very next cropping season with profuse flowering and set. The scions of Cauvery maintained usual genetic differences in time of flowering on the tenth day after rains save one scion, which coincide with Robusta on the eighth day. Grafting was effective during the month of July. Thus, top-working of old Robusta was successfully carried out thus both Robusta as well as Arabica crops can be harvested from same plant (Ramachandran et al., 1993).

heading: 8.7.7 Preference of growth regulators on graft union success in coffee
text: A field trial to investigate the role of growth regulators on the early union of grafts in coffee was laid out in two locations viz., Regional Coffee Research Station, Chundale and Cherunchal estate in Wayanad. The results have revealed that treating the cut end of the scions in different concentrations of plant growth regulators have no significant effect on early graft union. Under normal circumstances the union of stock-scion takes place in 45 days time, but the treatments have not hastened the union as per the observations made in the trial (Suresh Kumar et al., 1996).

heading: 8.7.8 Influence of canopy retention on suckers, success and growth of grafts in coffee
text: An investigation was carried out during 1993-94 to study the influence of canopy retention on success of grafting and growth of grafts in the rejuvenation of undesirable Robusta coffee. Results VEGETATIVE PROPAGATION revealed that collar pruning of plants in the early summer would lead to mortality of stump up to 17%. The success of grafting was not influenced by the amount of canopy retained at the time of grafting. Growth of grafts on stumps with 50% of canopy retained was on par with those on collar pruned stumps. The grafts on plants with full canopy had desirable growth characteristics like long internodes and poor stem girth. Thus it is observed that p artial canopy retention while grafting coffee helps in reducing the mortality, enhance sucker production and successful graft union (Suresh Kumar et al., 1998).

heading: 8.7.9 Grafting and its practical utility in coffee plantations
text: Grafting is an art of inserting a part of one plant into another in such a way that both will fuse together and continue their growth and yield satisfactorily. As per records available on grafting in coffee, the graft combination of CxR, Catimor, SIn.6, SIn.8 and SlIn.9 scions on Robusta and San Ramon root stocks were found most promising to get higher early yields. A maiden crop of 200 to 500 g of ripe fruit is harvested after 18 months of grafting. An yield of 5-15 Kg of ripe fruit per plant can be obtained after 28-30 months after grafting on a Robusta stock aged 15-20 years with Arabica or CxR scion (Anil Kumar and Srinivasan, 1999).

heading: 8.7.10 Rejuvenating coffee by grafting
text: Studies made on the effect of grafting to rejuvenate the coffee in the Wayanad coffee tracts is discussed in this paper. The investigations revealed that (1) grafted plants start to bear from the second year (2) treatment with hormones does not improve the graft take. Further it is also found that collar pruning results in the mortality (17%) of stumps. Partial retention of canopy helps to minimize the crop loss as well as mortality of the stumps. heading: 10.3.1 Successful establishment of Dadaps in coffee clearings
text: The Dadap branches are to be ringed at their bases, about a month prior to the proposed planting time. It is recommended that on the top cut end of the stakes a cap ofsome cattle dung mixed with urine is put on and covered with leaves or waxed paper. To minimize the bad effect of sun scorching, white washing is the best method. Retaining suckers all along the stem for 1 or 2 years will ensure a proper flow of sap even on the side of stem exposed to Western sun and there by minimize the scorching effect. If the stakes are planted in slant manner, the upper side of the stakes exposed to mid-day sun, resulting in more severe injury. The cuttings were 1 to 1.5 inches in diameter, 8 feet in length and 1.5 feet being underground (Pattabhiraman, 1953).

heading: 5 Embryo culture of three interspecific crosses in coffee
text: Immature embryos _ resulting from three interspecific crosses involving Coffea canephora cv. Robusta (selection no.274) as the common female parent and three indigenous wild species, C. travencorensis, C. bengalensis and C. wightiana as different make parents were cultured on modified MS medium. Both direct and indirect pathways regenerated plants. In the former pathway, the embryos matured and germinated directly into single plantlets. In the latter pathway, many plantlets were regenerated from single hybrid embryos, through callous and subsequent somatic embryogenesis (embryoidogenesis). Many hybrid plantlets rescued by the above methods are established in the soil and are being evaluated. These studies were taken up with a view to combining the agronomic properties of C. canephora with some useful characters of the wild species, especially the low caffeine content (Sreenath et al., 1992).

Plant Regeneration through high frequency eomatic embryogenesis from leaf tissues in gvo cultivars of coffee Planilets were regenerated through high frequency somatic embryogenesis in two coffee cultivars viz. §.2790 (Coffea arabica) and BR11 (Cc. canephora) from the leaf tissues. In all the experiments, MS agar medium supplemented with L-Cystein HCl (50 mg/l) and 3% sucrose was used, which was modified in various ways for experimentation. The calli were subcultured at 45-60 days interval to fresh medium of same or different composition. In §.2790, calli were induced from the leaf explants on MS medium supplemented with Kn (5 mg/l) and 2,4-D (1 mg/l). After 22 weeks of culture with 3 subcultures, the calli turned embryogenic on the medium of same composition. In BR-11, the calli were induced from the leaf explants on MS medium containing gamborg's-b-5 vitamins but supplemented with the same growth regulators as stated above. Calli were subcultured on the medium of same composition and after 18 weeks they were transferred to MS medium with 2 iP (2-5 mg/l) and 2, 4-D (0.2 mg/l). In this clone, the calli turned embryogenic after 9 weeks of culture on this medium.

Germination of embryoids into plantlets was achieved on half strength MS medium with 0.1 mg/1 kn. heading: 10 Hardening of in vitro raised plantlets
text: This note reports the simple procedure for hardening the plantlets of $.274 raised from stem culture through somatic embryogenesis. The experiment clearly indicated the importance of high humidity in hardening of coffee plantlets. Hence beaker covering was adopted. By adopting the procedure described here, around 90% of in vitro plantlets could be successfully hardened. Two points are important for good survival. 1. The in vitro plantlets should have reached the right stage with good root and shoot system. Provision for high humidity and low temperature and light intensity during the first 2-3 months of exvitro stage (Muniswamy et al., 1994).

Later the calli were subcultured to MS + 2,4-D (0.2 mg/1) + 2iP (2.5 mg/1) and after 2 months the calli turned darker, more compact and the proliferation almost stopped. heading: 16 Haploidy in Coffee
text: Various aspects of haploidy in coffee such as significance of haploids in coffee improvement programmes, frequency of occurrence of natural haploids among the coffee species, morphological and anatomical features and leaf rust tolerance of (di) haploids of Arabica, are dealt with. In vivo and in vitro approaches for production of haploids in coffee and the progress achieved in the coffee anther culture are also discussed (Raghuramulu and Prakash, 1995).

heading: 17 Somatic embryogenesis from cultured zygotic embryos of Coffea bengalensis
text: Coffea bengalensis is a wild indigenous species. It is wide spread and more adaptable to varied soil and climatic conditions and is characterized by low caffeine content or no caffeine. This note deals with the somatic embryo genesis and plant regeneration from the cultured zygotic embryos of C. bengalensis. In the present study, somatic embryogenesis and plant regeneration is achieved from the zygotic embryos of C. bengalensis. This will be useful for producing aseptic plants which in turn can be used in advanced studies like somatic hybridization for transferring the useful characters into commercial cultivars. This is the first report of inducing somatic embryogenesis and plant regeneration from cultured zygotic embryos of C. bengalensis (Muniswamy and Sreenath, 1996).

heading: 18 Effect of Kanamycin on callus induction and somatic embryogenesis in cultured leaf tissues of Coffea canephora Pierre (Robusta)
text: The effect of kanamycin at 0, 50, 100 and 400 mg/l in MS medium supplemented with NAA (0.1 mg/l) + BAP (1 mg/l) + L-cysteine HCl (50 mg/l) + sucrose (3%) on callus proliferation and somatic embryogenesis was studied using aseptic leaf tissues of Coffea canephora. Proliferation of callus subsequent embryogenesis was observed in a nearly all the explants cultured on kanamycin free medium. Callus development was reduced at 50 mg/l of kanamycin, while the callus induction was almost completely suppressed at 100 mg/I and higher concentrations. The results elucidated the sensitivity of coffee leaf tissues to kanamycin. As kanamycin resistance is widely used as a selectable marker in genetic transformation studies in plants, the possible utility of the present results in coffee transformation studies indicated (Muniswamy and Sreenath, 1996).

heading: 19 Callus proliferation from cultured roots in coffee (Brief Note)
text: The cotyledonary stage zygotic embryos were cultured initially on MS medium supplemented with ABA (1 mg/1) for 30 days for embryo maturation. The mature zygotic embryos of Coffee arabica cv. San Ramon and Cauvery (S.4348), C. bengalensis and C. canephora (S.274) were germinated by culturing on half strength MS medium (Murashige and Skoog, 1962) supplemented with 0.1 mg/1 of Kn. Roots from these aseptic plantlets were excised and cut into pieces of about 5-6 mm long and cultured on MS medium with NAA (1 mg/1), Kn (5 mg/1) and 3% sucrose. The pH of the medium was adjusted between 5.6 and 5.8 and solidified by adding 0.7% of bacteriological agar. The medium was sterilised at 121°C for 20 minutes and cultures were incubated at room temperature. All the four materials tested showed varying degrees of callusing response on MS medium with NAA and Kn. All the callused explants produced roots ranging from 1.4 to 2.6 cm in length (Muniswamy et al., 1996)

heading: 24 Effect of TIBA and BAP on Integument
text: Cultures of C x R cultivar of robusta coffee (Coffea canephora) Micropylar and chalazal sections ofintegument of CxR cultivar of Robusta coffee (Coffea canephora) were cultured on MS medium supplemented with different concentrations of TIBA and BAP (up to 10 mg/1) individually and in combinations. Microbial contamination was very low. The response was dependent on the maturity of the tissue as well as concentrations of TIBA and BAP. On the basal medium itself (without any growth regulator) vigorous callus proliferation was obtained in both micropylar and chalazal sections. Lower levels of TIBA appeared to promote callus proliferation, especially when young integument tissues were cultured. When the medium was supplemented with higher levels of TIBA and BAP (10 mg/1) callus proliferation was reduced substantially. When both TIBA and BAP were supplemented in the medium, there was progressive decrease in proliferation of the callus with the increasing concentrations of one or both of these growth regulators. Integument tissue of coffee with its aseptic nature, high, callusing ability and phytohormone autotrophy could be an excellent system for basic studies in cell proliferation and regeneration in addition to its physiological role (Harinath et al., 1997).

heading: 25 Biotechnology approaches for coffee improvement
text: The author while narrating biotechnology as a powerful tool, describes micro-propagation, anther culture, embryo rescue, somaclonal variation and cell line selection and protoplast fusion as various approaches for coffee improvement (Sreenath, 1998).

heading: 26 Tissue culture studies in coffee and _ its applications
text: In coffee, overall success in the tissue culture studies is quite encouraging. Plants are successfully produced from different tissues like embryo, anther, endosperm, stem and leaf. Tissue culture helps to overcome the limitations of the conventional breeding techniques. Several tissue culture methods can be extremely valuable in the improvement programme like disease resistance. Integration of these technologies will also reduce the time for varietal development and preserve haterozygosity and plasticity in coffee plantations (Muniswamy and Sreenath, 1999).

heading: 27 Direct shoot induction from cultured root explants of Coffea arabica
text: The procedure of obtaining direct shoot induction from cultured root explants of Coffea arabica is presented. Root explants were selected from aseptic plantlets regenerated from leaf tissue through callus and subsequent somatic embryogenesis. The root explants were cultured on MS (Murashige and Skoog) medium supplemented with 3% sucrose and different concentrations of NAA, 2,4-D, kinetin and BAP (benzyl adenine). All combinations produced callus but only halfstrength MS + 0.1 mg/l kinetin produced direct adventitious shoot buds after 4-5 weeks of culture. Multiple shoots were isolated from original root explants and cultured on MS + BAP (1 mg/litre) + kinetin (1 mg/litre). The shoots grew to 3-4 cm after 45-60 days. Some of the shoots produced roots simultaneously (Muniswamy & Sreenath, 1999).

heading: 28 Embryo culture in coffee techniques and applications
text: In coffee breeding programmes, embryo abortion is normally encountered in the seeds of unsuccessful crosses. The most useful and a rISSUE CULTURE popular application of zygotic embryo culture is rescuing incompatible hybrid crosses. In breeding programmes, inter- specific and_intergeneric crosses are frequently carried out to transfer valuable genes from wild species to cultivated Incompatibility is often encountered species. in such crosses and results in shriveled seeds containing aborted embryos (Muniswamy and Sreenath, 1999).

heading: 29 Preservation of coffee (Coffea arabica L.) by in vitro culture of zygotic embryos under slow growth conditions
text: Preservation of coffee (Coffea arabica L) by in vitro culture of zygotic embryos under slow growth conditions is reported. Zygotic embryos of Coffea arabica L. cv. Cauvery (Catimor) were cultured on MS based medium and on medium supplemented with different concentrations of abscissic acid. Cultures were maintained in dark at room temperature (25°C). The embryos were taken out at 5-6 months interval from above said culture conditions and transferred to germination medium containing BAP. The type of response depended on the different cultural conditions in which embryos were cultured and on concentrations of ABA in the medium. It was found that a higher concentration of ABA is effective for induction of embryo dormancy. Effective embryo germination was achieved on MS medium supplemented with BAP. The results confirm that embryos can be preserved without the loss of viability in presence of ABA even at room temperature up to two years without any subculture. heading: 32 Improved method of explant preparation for micro propagation of coffee through node culture
text: Disinfection of nodal explants of mature, field-grown coffee (cv. Catimor/Cauvery S. 4347) with different concentrations of NaOCl (0.05, 0.5 or 1%) or HgCl, (0.05, 0.1 or 1%) for 0, 5, 10 or 15 min resulted in the identification of conditions for efficient disinfection of explants. Nodal explants treated with 1% NaOCl for 15 min and 0.19% HgCl, for 5 min yielded best results among all the treatments tested. Foliar application of an antibiotic and fungicide mixture to orthotropous branches of mother plants improved the recovery of explants. Presence of stipules in the nodal explant was one of the factors responsible for poor recovery of explants. Treatment of nodal explants with very low concentration of HgCl, after the removal of stipules improved recovery, although the exposed axillary buds were sensitive to HgCl.. heading: 33 Plant regeneration through somatic embryogenesis from anther cultures of CxR cultivar of coffee
text: Plant regeneration through embryogenesis has been achieved from cultured anthers of C x R cultivar of coffee (an interspecific hybrid derivative of C. Congensis and C. canephora) (Robusta). Initially, flower buds were pretreated at different temperatures (5-25°C) for 24-72 h in dark. The anthers of uninucleate microscope stage where cultured on MS medium supplemented with different concentration of auxins, cytokinins and L-cysteine HC]. Anthers excised from the floral buds were pretreated at 5°C for 48 h followed by 10°C for another 24 h and cultured on MS medium with IBA and BAP (1 g/l each) for 90 days. After one more subculture on the same medium, they developed 1-2 mm wide, brown calli. After subculturing for another 90 days on MS medium with 2, 4-D (0.05 mg/l), IAA (0.5 mg/l) and Kinetin (8.6 mg/l), the calli grew further to 3-4 mm thickness. When these calli were transferred subsequently onto half-strength MS medium supplemented with NAA (0.05 mg/l), Kn (0.5 mg/l) and 2 x KNO,, nodular, friable embryogenic calli were produced after two months from the original brown callus. The embryogenic calli in turn differentiated into 3-4 white somatic embryos in another month. These embryogenic calli and embryos were further multiplied on MS medium with ABA (1 mg/l). The embryos were converted into plantlets on half-strength MS medium with 0.1 mg/l of Kn.

On these calli, embryogenic masses were induced after culturing for one more month on the same medium. The mature embryos germinated into plantlets after 3-4 subcultures at monthly intervals on half-strength MS medium supplemented with 0.1 mg/L of Kn. text: and plant regencration from leaf explants of Coffea bengalensis Roxb. : A wild coffee species In vitro adventitious shoot formation from foliar explants of Coffea bengalensis Roxb. was achieved. Among various combinations of growth regulators tested, N6 benzyl adenine (BA) was found to be the most effective in inducing shoot buds. Shoot buds are induced from the cut surface of foliar explants incubated on Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium supplemented with either BA alone (2.5 - 10 mg/l) or the combination of Indole -3-Acetic Acid (IAA, 0.1 - 1.0 mg/l) and BA (0.5 -5.0 mg/l). heading: 3 Procedure for generating silver stained AFp markers in coffee
text: Despite its economic and agricultural importance, coffee has not been _ benefited extensively from the technological developments, which have been applied for genetic analysis of other cash crops. There are only a few reports on the use of DNA based molecular techniques like RFLPs, RAPD and PCR for coffee genome analysis. Recently developed AFLP technique has tremendous potential in the marker assisted genetic improvement and genetic analysis and biodiversity evaluation of this commercially important crop. However, there is no report on AFLP analysis of coffee. Hence, studies were undertaken to optimize the procedure to generate silver stained AELP markers in coffee. Five selections of Coffea arabica, Coffea canephora and Psilanthus bengalensis (previously C. bengalensis were used a the study. DNA was isolated by SDS method. ‘AFLP procedure was performed as per the product anual supplied by M/s. Life Technologies Inc. with Se modifications. The amplified products were ov on a sequencing type vertical electrophoresis stem using 6% denaturing polyacrylamide gel. the amplified DNA bands were visualized by silver staining. In the five materials tested, AFLP technique could produce 20-50 amplified DNA bands, ranging in size from less than 200 pb to more than 2 kb. Many of the bands were polymorphic indicating the usefulness of the technique for genetic analysis of coffee.

text: S.288 an offspring of a putative spontaneous interspecific hybrid between tetraploid Coffea arabica (2n = 4x = 44) and diploid C. liberica (2n = 2x = 22) and 17 arabica coffee introgression lines (representing F2 and F4) derived from the 9 id e cross S.288 x Kent arabica were evaluated for introgression of C. liberica genetic material. In all analyte, een cpbinations were used in the analysis. -P profiles of introgressed lines were compared to five accessions each of C. arabica and C, liberica. A total of 137 polymorphic bands were scored among the 29 accessions analysed. The introgressed genotypes exhibited 102 marker bands consisting of 65 additional bands and 37 missing bands associated with introgression of C. liberica genetic material. C. liberica accessions of EA group (C. liberica var liberica of Guinean origin) seemed to be the likely progenitor in the origin of natural hybrid. Analysis of genetic relationships in the introgressed lines suggested that introgression was limited to few fragments. Segregation and wide variation in number of marker fragments in the F, and F, progenies were attributed to chromosome recombinations. The differences in the level of introgression between introgressed parent, F, and F, groups was not pronounced.

heading: 10 Morphological, biochemical and molecular characterization of ploidy variants in coffee for genetic improvement
text: The genus Coffea consists of more than hundred species of which only C. arabica (known as arabica coffee) and C. canephora (known as robusta coffee) are commercially cultivated. All the species of the genus Coffea are diploids and self-incompatible except C. arabica, which is an allotetraploid and selfcompatible species. In C. arabica, a series of ploidy variants of spontaneous origin were recovered and documented. In C. canephora, which is a diploid species, colchicine was used successfully to induce tetraploidy. In addition, a few spontaneous triploid plants conforming to either arabica or robusta Phenotype were also recovered. All the ploidy variants were studied for morphological characters such as leaf shape, leaf venation pattern, leaf anatomy, and stomatal features. The biochemical characters such as chlorophyll starch carbohydrate, phenol, sugar, amino acid cGnfent and flavonoid profile pattern also have been investigated. Molecular characterization of all the ploidy variants was carried out by using RAPD and PCR-RFLP and polymorphism was recorded. These results along with the utilization of the ploidy variants in coffee breeding program is discussed (Mishra et al., 2006)

text: " EST PCR-RELP, SNPs and SSR analysis An EST-based PCR-RFLP method was employed to gain insight into genome organization in eight allopolyploid Coffea arabica cultivars and seven diploid coffee species. In arabica, this condition could be explained by assuming the presence of duplicated loci in paralogous chromosomes and this was supported by considerable evidence of multiple loci SSR amplification. Based on the RFLP analysis, 12 EST loci were polymorphic. The level of polymorphism was higher in different species ‘compared to the arabica varieties. Sequencing of the amplified products revealed a SNP frequency of 0.021 among diploid species and of 0.007 among arabica varieties. We propose that the involvement of two genomes in C. arabica maintains a residual level of heterozygosity in the form of paralogous chromosomes, while the self-fertilization in this species tends to drive of homozygosity. The heterozygosity of paralogous chromosomes in arabica creates valuable polymorphism essential for species diversity and survival in various ecological niches, while self-fertility tends to preserve in homozygosity many genes of functional significance (Mishra et al., 2011).

Froehner) This study was conducted to compare the growth and yield of one of the commercial hybrid coffee cultivars (Coffea congensis x Coffea canephora) of robusta coffee established from somatic embryogenesis as well as conventional seedlings. Results indicated no _ statistically significant differences in the growth pattern or the cumulative yield between the somatic embryogenesis derived plants and the seedlings. The genetic fidelity of somatic embryogenesis derived plants and the mother plant was tested using Sequence Related Amplified Polymorphism (SRAP) markers. A total of 24 SRAP primers were employed for DNA analysis which produced a total of 153 clear, distinct and reproducible amplicons of variable size. Out of 24 SRAP primers, 9 primers produced amplification patterns which are identical between the mother plants and plants derived from somatic embryogenesis. Cluster analysis revealed more than 95% genetic similarity between the somatic embryogenesis derived plants and the mother plants indicating a high degree of genetic fidelity. The present study clearly demonstrates the usefulness of SRAP markers in genetic fidelity analysis of coffee (Muniswamy et al., 2017).

heading: 32 Diversity genotyping of Indian coffee (Coffea arabica L.) germplasm accessions by using
text: SRAP markers Coffea arabica L. is the only cultivated tetraploid species in the genus Coffea and it contributes more than 61% to the total world coffee production. Arabica produces superior beverage quality compared to robusta coffee but is susceptible to a number of pests and diseases. Improved varieties of arabica coupled with durable disease resistance can be achieved by incorporating novel sources of genetic variation from diverse germplasm sources. Assessment of genetic diversity within the germplasm pool is a prerequisite for estimating its true breeding potential. In the present study, 42 world germplasm accession of arabica were screened with co-dominant sequence-related amplified polymorphism (SRAP) markers. Twenty-one SRAP combinations amplified a total of 171 fragments of which 116 (67.83%) were polymorphic and 5.47% were rare alleles. Based on the Jaccard’s similarity coefficient the UPGMA dendrogram differentiated all the 42 accessions, with genetic similarity estimates ranging from 0.59 to 0.98. The model-based Bayesian analysis of population structure using the admixture model grouped the 42 arabica germplasm accessions into two ancestral groups. heading: 33 Genetic resources and breeding of Coffee
text: (Coffea spp.) Coffee is an important agricultural export commodity in many Asian, African and Latin American countries. It provides a livelihood for more than 125 million people worldwide: The genus Coffea comprises more than 125 species of which only 2 species Coffea arabica (arabica coffee) and C. canephora (robusta coffee) are commercially cultivated for beverage production. Climate change present sun precedented challenges to sustainable coffee cultivation on a global scale. Besides, both arabica and robusta coffee are subjected to biotic and abiotic stress conditions that limit their production and _ productivity. Although conventional breeding approaches are followed to attenuate some of these problems, they were slow and time-consuming. Furthermore, arabica coffee has a narrow genetic base and needs to be addressed immediately by incorporating diverse germplasm with potential agronomic values, using focused breeding programs. In both arabica and robusta, the full potential of germplasm has not been exploited. Recent progress in the biotechnological field particularly on molecular markers and new generation sequencing platform hold great promise to discover new genes and eee <<< accelerate coffee breeding programs. The progress achieved in coffee transgenic technology also has unparalleled opportunities to develop new cultivars with improved agronomic traits.

heading: 33 Genetic resources and breeding of Coffee

Recent progress in gene editing techniques has a significant impact on the genetic improvement of coffee. This chapter provides current and innovative information about coffee’s origin and distribution, genetic resource diversity and conventional breeding strategies and application. heading: 34 Gene expression analysis of Coffea arabica seeds processed under different post-harvest processing methods

Expression levels of 16 genes of interest were measured. These genes are involved in various cellular, metabolic and biochemical activities influencing levels of certain compounds, such as lipids, carbohydrates, caffeine and chlorogenic acid, associated with quality characteristics of the beverage. Microarray experiments were designed with cDNA probe sequences. Microarray data was analyzed to identify the differences in gene expression between two altitudes and between two variables; location and post-harvest treatment. Cluster analysis was carried out with samples showing similar patterns, which are characteristic to the group. With this approach, it was possible to identify the important genes in C. arabica seeds that have differential (increased or decreased) expression levels.

heading: 2 RAPD marker analysis reveals high genetic stability in high frequency somatic embryogenesis-derived plants of Robusta coffee (Coffea canephora)
text: This paper reports high frequency somatic embryogenesis, plant regeneration and _ high genetic stability in somatic embryo-derived plants (SEPs) of CR cultivar of robusta coffee (Coffea canephora Pierre) as assessed by RAPD markers. High frequency embryogenic calli were induced from the leaf explants from a 15 year-old superior plant (TL1) on MS medium supplemented with IAA (1 mg/l) and kinetin (5 mg/l). Somatic embryos were matured on MS medium with ABA (1 mg/l) and germinated on half strength MS medium supplemented with kinetin (0.1-1 mg/l). After hardening in net pots in a polytunnel and further growth in polybags in nursery, the SEPs were planted in the field. There was no detectable morphological variation in the SEPs. Fourteen SEPs established in the field were used for RAPD analysis. Genomic DNA was isolated from the fresh leaves of the mother plant (TL1) and one year-old SEPs by a modified SDS method. After initial screening of 25 arbitrary 10-base primers, 16 primers that gave distinct RAPD bands were used for further study. In total, 121 RAPD markers were obtained from 16 primers, out of which 120 markers were monomorphic across all the SEPs and the mother plant. One polymorphic marker of 1.4 kb size was obtained with the primer OPA- 14 in one SEP (Sreenath and Naidu, 2004).

heading: 5 Somatic embryogenesis and __ genetic homogeneity assessment in Coffea - Recent approaches
text: Coffee is one of the most preferred beverages consumed by millions of people throughout the world. It is cultivated in more than 80 countries in tropical and subtropical zones of Asia, Africa, and Latin America and provides livelihood to 125 million people worldwide. Among 125 coffee species known so far, only two coffee species, Coffea arabica (arabica coffee) and Coffea canephora (robusta coffee), are commercially cultivated for beverage production. Coffee is a perennial plant and therefore subjected to constant environmental Stress. However, during the last few decades, o _TISSUE CULTURE & MOLECULAR BIOLOGY sustainable coffee cultivation has been threatened by unprecedented climate change. This calls for unified efforts, including cutting-edge research and modified management practices. Although conventional breeding efforts have been developed to address some issues, emerging biotechnology research, especially in-vitro propagation technology, could augment the coffee cultivation landscape. Despite the tangible progress made in coffee tissue culture, there were some grey areas, such as the level of somaclonal variation and the genomic changes associated with somatic embryogenesis in coffee, which needs to be addressed imminently.

heading: 1 Agrobacterium-mediated transformation of coffee: An assessment of factors affecting gene transfer efficiency
text: Experimental conditions influencing Agrobacterium t-DNA delivery to coffee tissue were investigated using plasmid vector containing gusA (b-glucuronidase) intron reporter gene. Leaf explants, hypocotyls, zygotic and somatic embryos were used for co-cultivation experiments and transfer of t-DNA was assessed by analyzing the transient gusA gene expression. The study revealed that t-DNA delivery is preferentially targeted to distinct anatomical regions in different target tissues. In co-cultivated leaf explants, cut ends of the veins are the preferential target sites where as in zygotic and somatic embryos, hypocotyl and its adjacent region are the main target sites. Pre culture of recipient tissue and manipulation ofco cultivation conditions affected gene transfer efficiency and this is evident from transient gene expression assay. heading: 5 Recent advances in the genetic transformation of Coffee
text: Coffee is one of the most important plantation crops, grown in about 80 countries across the world. The genus Coffea comprises approximately 100 species of which only two species that is Coffea arabica (commonly known as arabica coffee) and Coffea canephora (known as robusta coffee), are commercially cultivated. Genetic improvement of coffee through traditional breeding is slow due to the perennial nature of the plant. Genetic transformation has tremendous potential in developing improved coffee varieties with desired agronomic traits, which are otherwise difficult to achieve through traditional breeding. During the last twenty years, significant progress has been made in coffee biotechnology, particularly in the area of transgenic technology. This paper provides a detailed account of the advances made in the genetic transformation of coffee and their potential applications (Mishra and Slater, 2012).

heading: 1.1 Effect of rain on coffee blossom
text: A field trial was laid out on young Arabica coffee (S. 1934) to elucidate information on the effect of rain on blossom. Rain in the morning hours affected the blossom-berry ratio adversely during all the 3 years of trial. No such adverse effect was noticed with afternoon rain. If rain came down on the open flowers, the pollen was largely lost. The stigma was more resistant and could still be fertilized the following day if there was some fresh pollen. Since pollination is over in the forenoon itself no adverse effect of afternoon rain was noticed (Awatramani and Satyanarayana, 1973).

Differences in the amount of rain received during various months of the years very large. Quantum of rain received during any particular month was not uniform during different years. heading: 2.5 Influence of soil cultivation methods in young coffee on soil moisture, weed suppression and organic matter
text: A field experiment was conducted on the CCRI farm for three consecutive years in a randomized block design with ten soil cultivation practices and three replications. Significantly higher stem girth, number of primary branches and bush spread were recorded in deep digging, scuffling, mulching with coir pith and green manure crop incorporation practices in all the years compared to control. Mulching with cherry husk and paddy straw did not improve the growth parameters of coffee. All mulches were found better than green manure crop, digging, scuffling and control in conserving the soil moisture during February. Whereas, weed suppression (as indicated by weed population, fresh and dry weed biomass) was higher in green manure treatments followed by mulch application compared to rest of the practices. Mulching, green manure crop incorporation, digging and scuffling Were found to improve the soil organic carbon content over the years. Control recorded the lowest soil moisture and organic carbon and the highest weed bio-mass which smothered the growth of young coffee variety C x R (Shivaprasad et al., 2005).

heading: 2.6 Effect of cultivation practices and green manure crops on soil moisture conservation and growth of coffee
text: A field experiment was conducted at the Research Farm of Central Coffee Research Institute, Chikkamagaluru during 2000-01 to 2003-04 to find out the effect of cultivation practices and green manuring on growth of coffee, soil moisture conservation, weed population and soil fertility. Results showed that significantly higher stem girth, number of primary branches and length of longest primary branch and bush spread were recorded with deep digging, scuffling, coir pith mulching and green manuring than control. Cherry husk and paddy straw mulching did not improve the growth parameters of coffee. Mulches were found better than green manure crops, digging, scuffling and control in conserving soil moisture during blossom period (March-April). Whereas, weed suppression was highest in green manure treatments followed by mulches as compared to other treatments. Mulches, green manure crops, digging and scuffling improved the soil organic matter (SOM) and available phosphorus in soil. Control recorded the lowest soil moisture, SOM, available phosphorus and the highest weed biomass which affected the vigour of young coffee (Shivaprasad et al., 2007).

heading: 5.1 Methods ofreplanting coffee- Abrief study
text: There are four simple methods for replanting. Replanting - This is the best method so far as the new plants are concerned. They will not stand any competition from established coffee and being young they are likely to get better attention. Interplanting - This consists of planting the seedlings of the selected plant material in between rows of existing old coffee. Competition from old coffee is severe in this method. Interlining-Simple - Alternate rows of old coffee are eliminated and new plants are planted in the row. The spacing within the row becomes flexible but the rigid spacing of the old lines will have to be maintained between the two rows. However, yield from the old coffee cannot be good as it is already exhausted. Interlining-Complex - In this case, while the rejuvenation is being attempted, old coffee also gets a fresh lease of life. This appears to be the best method as, although there would be any crop in the first year, the sucker from the collar pruned plants will bear better crops from second year onwards thus maintaining the plot while a portion of it getting rejuvenated (Hanumantha, 1964). j

heading: 6.7 Shade cum fruit yielding avocado under coffee ecosystem
text: Avocado is one of the most commonly preferred shades grown tree crop under Coffee ecosystem. In view of that, Peninsula of Nicoya and Cost Rica farmer was rated avocado (Persea americana L. Mill) is a primary shade tree crop under coffee plantation at the level of 66.3 per cent and it ranked as a fourth position after the Inga spp., Guazuma ulmifolia and Cordia alliodoara. Hence, the avocado is a commercially important shade cum fruit yielding tree under coffee ecosystem which has cultivating both in humid tropic as well as subtropical climates of throughout the world. The tree is basically grown as the forest species but later on as a shade growing tree under coffee cultivation because of high nutritional and medicinal values of fruit and it makes for wider diversity. Thereafter it was entered into the other parts of the world from Central America and Mexico. The tree is of multipurpose in nature and also helps to avoid the soil and water erosion by way of its wider spread canopy. Generally, Avocado leafs reduce the beating action of rain drops which in-turn minimize the soil erosion. The soil enrichment by adding the leaf litter continuously is an advantage in the coffee plantations. It yields in the additional economic returns after three to five years of establishment.

heading: 7.5 Spacing for Arabica
text: Maximum yield may obtain at densities where competition between the plants is less. Maximum density giving maximum yield is the density at which yield per unit area due to addition of extra plants is offset by loss due to decrease in weight per bush. Spacing in coffee depends on more than one factor. There is a strong genotype -density fertility interaction. The species /cultivars of coffee used, pruning /training system adopted, type of soil, rainfall pattern - whether irrigated or not etc. However under Indian conditions spacing of 1.8 x 2.7 m is the best for Arabica var. heading: 7.13 The effect of modified pruning and planting
text: Systems on growth, yleld, labour use efliciency and economics of Arabica coffee — The economics of colfee plantations is onal linked to pruning, which can improve the canopy architecture and thereby increase use efficiency. However, in India, recommended pruning methods viz., light, medium and hard pruning on Arabica coffee plantations have been highly labour intensive. The labour constitutes about 60 % towards cost of cultivation of coffee. In this study, the modified pruning and planting systems were investigated on Arabica coffee cv. Chandragiri and assessed for growth, yield and labour productivity at Central Coffee Research Institute, India over a period of nine consecutive years (2010-2018). Experimental results revealed that all the growth attributes and clean coffee yield were significantly influenced by modified planting systems (hedge row and paired row) and pruning methods (cyclic and rock-n-roll). heading: 7.13 The effect of modified pruning and planting
text: Correlation coefficient data indicated that growth parameters had shown positive and significant correlation with clean coffee yield (CC) due to effect of modified pruning and planting systems except plant height. Mean data showed that adoption of modified pruning and planting systems helped to get higher clean coffee yield (1316 kg/ha), about 22-55 % of labour savings and maximum cost:benefit ratio of 1:2 could be achieved over traditional system of pruning and planting system. These results suggest that modified pruning methods facilitate vertical growth of coffee plants and thereby provide huge scope for high density planting system without compromising the yield. Further, an efficient labour force and adequate supply of human labour is the basic requirement for successful commercial cultivation of coffee. Hence, modified pruning methods such as cyclic and rock-n-roll pruning could be an option for improving the labour productivity of Indian coffee plantation (Gokavi et al., 2021). heading: 8.7 Drip irrigation
text: A study on the impact of drip irrigation on 4 year old S.274 was carried out for 2 years to find out its effect on flowering, fruit set, retention and crop yield. Five different types of emitters viz., oneway dripper (2.28 LPH), two-way dripper (8.09 LPH), micro tube (6.35 LPH), micro sprinklers (14.60 LPH) and pitcher with a discharge rate of 1 L/day were used for irrigation during December to March-April. The effect of these irrigation treatments was discernible as reflected on the average fruit set, retention and crop yields. A highest yield increase of 146% was obtained from micro sprinkler irrigation, followed by two-way dripper irrigation (58.9%) over the unirrigated control. These results appeared highly promising, considering the age of the bushes (Sopal Ram et al., 1992).

heading: 8.13 Influence of micro irrigation and drip fertigation practices on yield and quality parameters of Robusta coffee (Coffea canephora).
text: A field experiment was_ initiated in established Robusta coffee plantation with different levels of drip fertigation viz., 75, 100, 125 and 150% of recommended dose of fertilizers to study the influence of micro-irrigation and drip fertigation on yield and yield parameters of coffee at Central Coffee Research Institute. Results showed that drip fertigation with 125% recommended dose of fertilizers recorded significantly higher bearing nodes per branch (24.27) and pin heads/branch (623.29) which was on par with teeatment having drip fertigation of 100% of recommended dose of fertilizers (23.42 and 600.13 respectively) and 75% of recommended dose of fertilizers (23.12 and 591.42 respectively) over the control. Similarly, significantly higher clean coffee yield (1008 kg/ ha) was recorded in the treatment with 125% recommended dose of fertilizers drip fertigation and it was on par with the treatment received 100% recommended dose of fertilizers through drip fertigation (960 kg/ha) which was followed by 75% recommended dose of fertilizers through drip fertigation (671 kg/ha). text: Control usually involves reduction of the weed stand sufficiently to prevent competition with coffee. The quantum of control is generally a balance between its economy and injury or loss weeds may cause to coffee. Dowpon appears effective against the common grasses when applied at 10 Ib/acre either in one or two applications. It has to be sprayed when grasses are in active growth phase. The treated plots continue to remain free of grass weeds anywhere from 4 to 12 months. Combination with other weedicides having selective action can achieve kill of grasses and other weedsdicots. In this case extra care is essential to ensure that spray drift does not affect coffee or young shade trees. Dowpon applied at 5 lb. and above per acre affects dadaps. This is noticed generally 2 to 4 months after application and the effect persists for a considerable time. Regarding persistence of Dalapon the chemical could last much longer under dry conditions. Dadaps commenced to show phytotoxic symptoms from September-November onwards though it was applied during May-August. Dowpon, which may enter into dadap trees by root absorption, may continue to exert the toxic effects for a long period. On account of the bad effects seen on dadaps large scale use of Dowpon for suppression of grass in coffee fields is not recommended (Narasimhaswamy et al., 1962).

Biology and Distribution of the Invasive Alien Weed Mikania micrantha-A review Invasion by alien perennial weed Mikania created a serious problem in micrantha has i Southeast Asia. This climbing vine possesses very fast growth rate and could multiply from seed and vegetative parts. It climbs on other plants, create a dense cover and block sunlight thereby damage or kill the other plant. It compete for water, soil nutrient and release allele-chemicals inhibiting growth of plants. The weed creates economic loss to plantation, horticultural crops, displaces and kills native vegetation. It is designated as one of the worst invasive plants of the world. M. micrantha is native to Central and South America and is a harmless plant in its native range. It was widely distributed by man to tropical areas of Africa, Asia, Australia and many different countries. The growth of the weed depends on availability of sunlight and soil moisture. M. Micrantha flowers during cool dry season and produces large number of viable seeds. The seed losses its viability with time.

text: The results obtained from the study carried out to understand the possible utility of Zeolites in coffee effluent abatement were encouraging as they indicated effective lowering of chemical and biological oxygen demands of the effluent by treatment with small quantities of Zeolites in combination with agricultural lime. text: Indian Coffee Plantations: Evaluation of different machineries to improve labor use efficiency and to reduce drudgery Field evaluation of different machineries was carried at Central Coffee Research Institute (CCRI) and Coffee Research Sub Station (CRSS), Chettalli during the year 2012-16. Results of field evaluation on different spaying system indicated that significantly higher field efficiency was observed with Multi Utility Track Vehicle spraying with 4 spray lance (0.557 ha/hour) and it was on par with Centralized Spraying System with 14 spray lance (0.510 ha/hour). Lower field efficiency was observed with power tiller spray system (0.410 ha/ hour) with 8 lance. Similarly, the labor requirement for Multi Utility Track Vehicle system was less (9 labors/day) as compared to Centralized Spraying System (28 labors/day) and PT (16 labors/day), which resulted in labor cost savings to the extent of 211% as compared to Centralized Spraying System. Mechanical weed cutter was found to be more efficient and economic in terms of cost (Rs.829 per acre) over manual weeding (Rs.2800 per acre) and chemical weeding (Rs.1075). Man days utilized for mechanical weed cutter was also much lesser (1.5 per acre) than manual weeding (10 per/acre) and chemical weeding (3.3 per/acre) respectively.
