heading: 12.17 Trends in area, production and productivity of coffee across the major coffee growing states in India
text: India has been ranking among top seven producers of coffee in the world, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu being the major coffee producing states in the country. However, there has been a consistent fluctuation in the production in the recent years across the states due to changing climate conditions. The paper aims to examine the trends in planted area under coffee, bearing area under coffee, production and productivity of coffee in India by using compound growth rate analysis with the 18 years time series data. It also analyses the area and productivity effect as preliminary determinants of coffee production. The major issues and challenges relating to production and productivity of coffee have also been dealt with. text: The lime requirement of 33 high-level laterite soils of West Coast where coffee is being grown was investigated. text: South India An exploratory trial to determine the absorption pattern of Nitrogen from Urea sprays, the optimum concentration of Urea at which considerable quantities of Nitrogen can be supplied to coffee as foliar sprays was conducted at the Central Coffee Research Institute. heading: 5.2.2 Biurct toxicity in Arabica coffee
text: Effect of foliar sprays and soil applications of Urea containing concentrations of Biuret was studied using 15 month old Coffea arabica Cv. Kents seedlings. This was compared with foliar sprays and soil applications of pure Biuret and available samples of Urea. Foliar applications of Urea containing Biuret at 2.5% and above and soil applications of Urea with 10% Biuret and above resulted in Biuret toxicity. The symptoms of toxicity and the sequence of its development have been described. While for foliar sprays, coffee was found to be tolerant to Biuret contents of up to about 2% in Urea, that for soil applications an accumulation of about 1.5 g of Biuret in the soil appeared critical. The present study showed coffee to be more sensitive to Biuret toxicity than Citrus, Tea and vegetable crops (Iyengar et al., 1976).

text: Soil incu bation st j i Studies with varying rates of Phosphorus ke: at different fixed levels of Zinc revealed that Phosphorus even at 2400 ppm, did not alter the extractable soil Zinc appreciably, Possibly due to the presence of Zinc mostly as Organically bound or occluded Zinc in the soil under experimentation. The data indicated that Sulphur deficiency could not manifest even under the conditions of continuous use of fertilizers containing low or no Sulphur component in them (Krishnamurthy and Ananda, 1982).

heading: 5.5.2 Sulphur status of soils cropped to coffee
text: (Koppa and Mudigere) Survey of Sulphur status through soil analysis in 2 coffee growing sub-zones revealed Ta that 70% of the soil samples tested had available Sulphur determined as heat soluble Sulphur well above the critical limit revealing that there was no immediate possibility of Sulphur being a limiting factor under the present day use of high analysis fertilizers. This could perhaps be due to high organic matter status of coffee soils as revealed by the data and incidental uses of sulphates of Copper and Zinc (Krishnamurthy and Ananda, 1984).

heading: 5.5.3 Evaluation of extractants to assess the availability of soil Sulphur
text: Evaluation of some of the commonly used extractants to predict the availability of soil Sulphur to Arabica vis-a-vis heat soluble Sulphur indicated that heat soluble Sulphur was present in higher amounts followed by Ammonium acetate or Ammonium acetate- Acetic acid extractable Sulphur. Sulphur extracted by Bray- I reagent, 0.15% Calcium chloride or cold water was comparatively less. Correlation co-efficient worked out revealed that heat soluble Sulphur and Sulphur extractable by Ammonium acetate- Acetic acid, cold water and Ammonium acetate had significant correlation with plant Sulphur. Bray-I extracted Sulphur had poor correlation. This study suggested that Ammonium acetate - Acetic acid or Ammonium acetate could be employed to assess the availability of soil Sulphur to C. arabica in routine soil testing programme (Ramamurthy and Raju, 1987).

text: Mineral nutrients are elements acquired by the plants primarily in the form of inorganic ions from the soil. After being absorbed by the roots, the mineral elements are translocated into various parts of the plant, where they are utilized in numerous biological and metabolic functions. Macro and micro nutrients are involved in numerous plant metabolic processes; foliar analysis has proven useful in establishing fertilizer schedules that sustain yields and ensure the food quality of many crops. Consequently, the current field experiment is conducted to know the influence of organic and integrated nutrient management practices (INM), on nutrient status of leaf major nutrient composition and yield of Robusta coffee. The average bean yield remained higher (1230 kg/ha) in INM mode of nutrition compared to that of exclusive organics (1101 kg/ha) (Hareesh et al., 2021).

heading: 3.2 Physiological studies on flowering in coffee under South Indian conditions: Changes in water content, growth rate, respiration and
text: carbohydrate metabolism of flower buds during bud enlargement and anthesis A comparative study has been made on the progressive changes in the water content, growth rate, respiration and carbohydrate metabolism in mature flower buds (just before blossom showers); during the enlargement of flower buds (after blossom showers) and in the fully opened flowers on the blossom day, in Arabica and Robusta coffee plants grown under field conditions at Central Coffee Research Institute. The results are described and discussed in detail. The data indicate that among the two species, Robusta coffee appear to be physiologically more efficient not only with respect to absorption of more quantities of water from soil by the roots (after blossom showers) and its supply to the flower buds for their renewed growth, ——s 197) F } i Lad but also the flower buds took up more oxygen with lesser availability of respirable substrate (reducing sugars) in the initial days of flower bud enlargement with the advent of blossom showers, as compared to the flower buds of Arabica coffee. This physiological efficiency in Robusta coffee plant offers an intriguing possibility to the plant breeder for its continuous use in breeding programmes. to evolve new cultivars with these advantageous features (Gopal et al., 1975).

heading: 6.2 Role of carbohydrates in growth and development
text: Carbohydrates play a dominant role in crop production. Carbohydrates are the resultant products of photosynthesis. In coffee rate of photosynthesis will be maximum when the light density is about 2000-foot candles. Light intensity beyond 6000-foot candles produces an adverse effect on the metabolic activities of plant. The deficiency of carbohydrates in the plant leads to berry drop and bean disorders (black bean and black jellow). heading: 9.1 Transpirational studies on coffee
text: Experiments to evaluate transpirational loss from species and varieties of coffee, in case of Arabica, it was observed that 34% of water lost by transpiration in 24 hours period occurred from upper surface of leaves. Seedlings affected by leaf disease and brown eye spot transpired 154.4% and 124.3% respectively more than healthy Arabica seedlings though the area of fungal infection was <10% to the total leaf area. C. liberica transpired more than canephora, arabica and excelsa in the order stated. Out of 2 commercial species tested canephora and Arabica, the former registered higher transpirational loss than the latter. Spraying both surfaces of leaf of arabica with 2:2:40, Bordeaux mixture checked the rate of transpiration effectively than other treatments including control (Gopalakrishnan and Ananth, 1960).

Conversely, the transpiration rate is a very insensitive indicator and cannot be used to determine irrigation requirements. Net photosynthesis is severely affected by small water deficits, a decrease of about 50% being expected from a 92-80% drop in relative turgidity of the leaves. The ratio T/P expresses the relative effect of water stress on transpiration and photosynthesis and therefore is a valuable selective parameter for drought resistance and has a great value under the perspective of agricultural economy. heading: 2.1.20 Variability among the sibmated progenies of theree arabica selections for resistance to coffee leaf rust
text: Coffee leaf rust incidence was recorded from an experimental plot of sib-mated progenies of arabica coffee cultivars viz., Sln.5B. Sln.7.3 and SIn.10 for a period of five years from 1999 to 2003. The maximum mean percentage of rust incidence recorded was 79.73 in SIn.10 (Sib. 3), 41.75 in SIn.5B (Sib. 3) and 31.96 in SiIn.7.3 (Sib. 4). Variability in terms of rust incidence from 0.95% to 79.73% was found among the sib-mated progenies, indicating the wide variation of the genotypes for resistance to coffee rust pathogen. Of the three arabica selections studied, siblings of Sln.10 had highest rust incidence (79.73%) whereas the progenies of SIn.5B and Sln.7.3 showed certain level of resistance as indicated by low disease index. A rust incidence level of less than 10% was recorded in the sib-mated progenies of SIn.5B (SIn.1, 2 and 4) and SIn.7.3 (SIn.1, 2, 3, 5, 8 and 11). These siblings, with low rust scale could be exploited further in the breeding programme for coffee leaf rust disease resistance. Yield data indicated a variation in yield ranging from 398 to 927 kg/ha (clean coffee) among the sib-mated progenies. Among the siblings and within the selection, the yield varied from 476 to 912 kg/ha in SIn.5B; from 398 to 927 kg/ha in SIn.7.3 and from 580 to 862 kg/ha (clean coffee) in SIn.10 (Daivasikamani et al.,2005). ___ Rainfall during March/April, number 007 UU meee f it

Around four hundred rust spore samples collected from the differentials, A type” plants and coffee fields from diverse locations in the traditional coffee growing areas of South India were differentiated from 2004 onwards. The rust race trapping strategy adopted in the present study proved to be very effective and it is of interest that as many as thirty-four rust races could be differentiated within a short period of eight years, among which fifteen were new races. heading: 2.2.5 Influence of abiotic factors on coffee leaf rust disease caused by the fungus Hemileia vastatrix Berk. & Br. under changing climate
text: Coffee being a perennial crop, harbours pathogens on all parts of the plant continuously and the intensity of diseases increase under favourable conditions. Coffee Leaf Rust (CLR) caused by the fungus Hemileia vastatrix Berk. & Br. is one among the most important diseases affecting coffee all over the world. Coffea arabica L. is well known to be highly susceptible to leaf rust (Wellman, 1953; Waller, 1982). The infection leads to foliage and berries loss up to up to 50 and 70% respectively (Sudhakar et al., 2014). Under favourable conditions, the disease appears after the blossom showers in March/April. Foliage present at that period is mostly of the previous season and the fungus remains dormant on these infected leaves during the dry weather from December to February and sporulates to form fresh uredospores after the blossom showers (Muthappa et al., 1989). heading: 2.4.1 Effect of foliar application of Nickel compounds and Zinc Sulphate on the incidence of coffee leaf rust
text: Coffee leaf rust (CLR), caused by Hemileia vastatrix, is a major disease affecting Coffea arabica worldwide, including India. While CLR management relies on fungicide use and resistant cultivars, biological control remains underexplored. Field studies identified a hyperparasite, Lecanicillium lecanii, colonizing CLR lesions and inactivating uredospores. In vitro studies showed that L. lecanii culture filtrate (CF) significantly (P < 0.01) inhibited uredospore germination. In vivo, uredospore discoloration (white) occurred within a week in treatments where L. lecanii was applied 24 - 48 hours before CLR inoculation. Among 11 Arabica cultivars, SIn.3 (S.795) showed the highest hyperparasitization (63%), followed by Sln.12 (51%). These findings suggest L. lecanii could be used as a prophylactic biological control for CLR, particularly in moderately tolerant or susceptible varieties (Divya et al., 2024).

heading: 5.1.2 Viability of Rhizoctonia solani
text: Rhizoctonia solani, coffee strain, which causes collar rot or damping off of coffee seedlings in the nursery stage, is a soil inhabitant. The outcome of the result indicates that the sclerotia of R. solani burried in the soil survive for more than one year in the seed beds. The survived sclerotia act as the primary inoculum for the next season and this leads to the perpetuation of the pathogen in the soil. Therefore, it is suggested to use the fresh soil every year to prepare the seed beds after removing the old soil completely (Venkatasubbaiah and Safeeulla, 1983). tts

heading: 5.1.3 Importance of inoculum density of
text: Rhizoctonia solani An attempt was made to relate the inoculum density and disease expression in collar rot infection of coffee seedlings. Results reveal that there was a linear relationship between inoculum density and disease expression up to inoculum densities of 25% and there after a gradual decline in infection was observed in both sterilized and unsterilized soils. While maximum infection (100%) was apparent from 5-25% inoculum density in sterilized soil, whereas between 25- 50% inoculum densities in unsterilized soil maximum infection was observed. The disease incidence was less in unsterilized soil than in sterilized soil. The decrease in disease incidence at higher inoculum densities might be a reflection of the operation of auto-inhibition by the propagules. Based on the fact that 5% inoculum density in sterilized soil would suffice to achieve 100% infection, it can be speculated that this represents the threshold value (Venkatasubbaiah and Safeeulla, 1983).

heading: 5.1.4 In vitro screening of Trichoderma spp.
text: against collar rot pathogen The success of establishing new plantations of a perennial crop like coffee mainly depends on the use of healthy seedlings with good vigour for planting. For this purpose, it is most essential to protect the seedlings in the primary and secondary nursery beds from attacks of pest and diseases. Coffee seedlings at the nursery stage are susceptible to fungal diseases. In the present study four Trichoderma spp. were tested for their ability to inhibit soil borne pathogen Rhizoctonia solani Kuhn. causing collar rot in coffee seedlings. Dual culture technique revealed that T: hamatum (75.68%) highly inhibited mycelial growth of pathogen followed by T: koningii (65.92), T: viride (57.90%) and T. harzianum (52.71%) respectively. heading: 5.2.3 Histopathological and histochemical changes due to Rhizoctonia solani in coffee seedlings
text: Rhizoctonia solani, the collar rot pathogen of coffee seedlings, penetrated the host tissue forming infection cushion and infection pegs. The fungal spread was both inter and intra cellular. Among various tissues, epidermis and cortex were more vulnerable to fungal invasion. The establishment of pathogen lead to the formation of sclerotia in the cortex. Distortion of the collar tissue and formation of cavities in the cortex was the common anomaly. The histochemical analysis of the infected collar tissue indicated reduction in insoluble polysaccharides, starch, protein and nucleic acid content (Venkatasubbaiah et al., 1984).

text: Gradual declining of plants resulted in periodical removal of several dead plants. It was observed that the declining plants were infected by red root disease fungus, Poria hypolateritia Berk. Among the four root diseases, brown root disease caused by Phellinus noxius is predominantly observed and affects both Arabica and Robusta cultivars. Presently, brown root disease is managed by adopting integrated disease management practices which also includes drenching of the fungicide carbendazim 50 WP. Of late, it has been observed that the ineffectiveness of the fungicide may be due to the acquired resistance by the pathogen against the fungicide. In addition, most importantly carbendazim is included in draft order of banned pesticides list. Hence, exploring an alternative fungicide is need of the hour. text: In the recent years, symptoms of berry rot were observed on field plants of Coffea arabica L. during rainy seasons in the farm of Central Coffee Research Institute, Balehonnuru, India. heading: 15.23 Air-spora of coffee plantations
text: The qualitative and quantitative changes in the air-spora of coffee field at CCRI was studied continuously from 1* January to 31* December, 1988 using Burkard volumetric spore trap kept at a height of 1.98 m above the ground level. About 22 types of fungal spores along with ascospores, basidiospores, conidiospores, fern spores, hyphal fragments, insects, insect hairs and scales, pollen grains, plant hairs, trichomes and xylem elements, smut spores, uredospores and dust particles caught in the trap were considered under group classified and others not included in the above categories were considered under group unclassified to estimate the quantum of total air-spora. Spore concentration was maximum during the months of September and October and minimum in April and May corresponding to wet and dry conditions respectively. Diurnal periodicity of the total airspora exhibited peak concentration between 0 and 6.00 hours. Cladosporium, ascospores and basidiospores constituted 83% of the total air-spora. However, it may be concluded that there is no spore free season in coffee plantation (Hanumantha et al., 1991).

heading: 18.1 Abnormal growth of shoots on scions of
text: , Arabica coffee grafted on to Robusta root stock Coffee, both Arabica and Robusta can be rejuvenated by collar pruning the old and unproductive plants and allowing new shoots to develop from the stump. For this, the old plants are stumped at a height of nine inches from the ground on receipt of first summer showers and when the new suckers develop, two or three sturdy ones are retained for further training one into a healthy plant. The advantage here is that the root system is already well developed and so the new shoot comes to bearing earlier than if a plant had been raised from a seed. While doing such type of rejuvenation pruning, it is also possible to graft shoot material from high yielding disease resistant varieties by wedge cleft grating method (Anonymous, 2000). For this, the healthiest among the suckers, of about pencil thickness, that develop during the summer period is selected and a horizontal cut is made just below the first node. On this a straight downward cut to a depth of 1 to 1.5 cm is made, which acts as the cleft. The scion that is to be grafted, of the same thickness as the scion, is selected and a single node cutting is made. The lower tip of this is cut into the shape of a wedge and then inserted into the cleft and the union is tied into place using strips of polythene.

text: The egg to adult a op oa period in the laboratory on cut Arabica collee s - was 71 to 90 days, whereas in the field on Ara te plants, it was 142 to 178 days. Observations on re emergence pattern of adult beetles revealed that t : beetles emerge in two batches in a year. The tota life cycle may vary depending on the condition of the coflee stem. Possibly the beetles that emerged during the summer flight lay eggs and develop into adults and emerge in the winter flight season and vice versa. The larval development is influenced toa great extent by the microclimate and the condition of the host stem. Moisture availability and the size of the stem appear to be the two major factors’ deciding the duration of development from egg to adult. Invariably, the borer takes longer time to complete its life cycle on coffee plants in the field. This may be due to the fact that the borer adults select bigger plants for egg laying and since the plants are in the field they do not dry up as fast as the cut stems used in the laboratory. The presence of two distinct broods in a year is suspected which needs further studies. Since a better understanding of the entire biology can help in developing better management strategies for the control of this pest, the findings on the biology are presented in this paper (Seetharama et al., 2005). heading: 1.3.7 Biology of Apenesiasahyadrica, a parasitoid of the coffee white stem borer
text: The parasitoid, Apenesia sahyadrica was multiplied in the laboratory on white stem borer larvae for the first time in India. Males were smaller in size compared to females, winged and black in color with 6.24 + 0.19 mm length, whereas females were wingless, dark brown in color with a length of 6.53 + 0.18 mm. The gravid female searched for the host larvae and paralyzed it before egg laying. More numbers of eggs were laid on the posterior lateral side of the host larvae. The average number of eggs laid was 8.03 + 0.49 eggs/day with a range of 1 to 15 eggs. The mated female could lay on an average of 17.52 +1.11 eggs in one single clutch. A female during her life span, laid 53.64 + 3.06 eggs. The eggs were elongate, oval, translucent, pale white in color, measuring 0.78 + 0.01 mm in length and 0.300.004 mm in width. Incubation period was less than 5 days. There were four larval instars with a total larval period of 10 to 12 days. The larval instars could be differentiated by the size and number of dentates. Pupation was inside the cocoon and pupal period lasted for 17.83 + 1.91days. The total duration of life cycle was 31.36 + 0.67 days. The sex ratio was generally one male to five females. Longevity of female wasps was 66.48 + 3.66 days and that of males was 7.96 + 0.3 days (Seetharama et al., 2007). fre

Different concentrations ranging from 0.05 to 7.5 ml/L for Lindane 20 EC, 0.25 to 3.5 ml/ L for Chlorpyrifos 20 EC and 0.2 to 3 ml/L for Carbosulfan 25 EC were tested in the laboratory. heading: 2.2.3 Varietal preference of Coffee Berry Borer
text: The present study was conducted in the laboratory and field to know the preference of berry borer of different coffee varieties like C. canephora, C. arabica, C. liberica and C. eugenioides. The laboratory experiment was replicated eight times, and each replication contained 80 seeds, a mixture of 20 parchment seeds painted with different colours. The preference to the seeds of C. arabica was significantly higher, followed by C. canephora, E eau e baie: 7 C. racemosa and Instly C. liberica in the laboratory condition. However, the fecundity of the beetle was higher in © cancphora followed by C. arabica. In C. liberica and C. racemosa the fecundity was very low. The observations on the field showed a significant preference of beetles for C. arabica followed by C. cancphora, C. liberica and C. eugenioides. However, there was no significant difference in fecundity between C. canephora and C. arabica. The fecundity in C. canephora and C. arabica was significantly higher than C. eugenioides and C. liberica. Thus, the above studies indicated that there is no significant difference in the susceptibility of C. arabica and C. canephora to the berry borer. However, among the species screened C. arabica and C. canephora are more prone to borer attack than other species. heading: 2.2.4 Observations on the position of attack of the berry borer
text: To study the mode of attack of the coffee berry borer, an observational trial was conducted at the Kalyanamandiram estate, Puliyarmala, Kalpetta, Kerala. Twenty five plants in the infested estate were observed, dividing their height into upper, middle and lower tiers. One branch each’ from each tier was examined for infestation, counting the total number of fruits and infested fruits. Likewise, the infestation percentages, at the top of the branches, middle of the branch and base of the branch were calculated by counting the infested fruits, selecting two clusters at the top, middle and two nodes adjacent to the main stem. Similarly, plants were observed to find out, whether the position of the plant in the estate, affected infestation. Every 5" plant at the road side i.e., to the periphery of the plantation was examined for infestation. Plant infestation and fruit infestation were recorded. Likewise, leaving 10 plants in a row to the interior of the plantation, similar observations were recorded. Observations showed the plants positioned at the periphery of the plantation are more to pest attack as evident from both plant and fruit infestation (Vijayalakshmi et. al., 2000).

heading: 4.3.16 Biological control with exotic as well as indigenous natural enemies
text: os While defining the biological control, which is the regulation of an organism's population density by natural enemies, the paper elaborates further the overall phenomenon of natural control. Additional control by introducing natural enemies or by manipulating available natural enemies or the environment is also brought about. The author groups the natural enemies into parasites, predators and pathogens. How biological control in coffee mealy bug has been brought about is discussed in the paper (Chacko, 1987).

heading: 4.3.17 Mealy bugs of coffee and their control measure
text: Mealy bugs are major sucking pests of coffee. They occur both on Arabica and Robusta, se if gas i but a major pest of Robusta. Among a number of species of mealy bugs that attack coffee, the ae common ones include Planococcus citri (Risso) anc P. lilacinus (Cockerell). The biology of the mealy bug has been described and the ecological a that help the pest attack and the damage to coffee have been narrated. Apart from different control measures against the mealy bug, bio-control with the help of exotic predator i.¢., Australian ladybird beetle, Cryptolaemus montrouzieri and Leptomastix dactylopii the parasitoid are dealt with in this paper. Further indigenous natural enemies although are noticed are unable to exert desired control over the mealy bugs (Venkataramaiah and Ramaiah, 1988).

text: Bioefficacy of some neem formulations viz, Econeem 0.3%, Gronim 0.15%, Neem Limnoids EC and Azadirachtin 1500 ppm alone at the dosages of 15 ml and 25 ml/litre, the same neem formulations at the dosage of 10 ml/litre in combination with half the recommended dose of Quinalphos 20 AF (0.75 ml/litre) and full dose of Quinalphos 20 AF (1.5 ml/litre) was evaluated against coffee mealy bug, P citri (Risso) (Homoptera: Pseudococcidae) on three-year old Coffea arabica plants at the Coffee Research Station, Chikkamangaluru. heading: 4.3.29 Attendant ants and activity of Spalgis epius
text: The mealy bug, Pcitri is always found in attendance with different species of ants, simple tests revealed the interference of the ants with the activity of Spalgis epius. The aggressiveness of the ants and S. epius population appeared to have a negative relationship. The base data on the activity of S. epius on mealy bug infested branches of the coffee plants attended by three different species of ants indicated that the ant species belonging to the genus Crematogaster interfered more with the predetor activity than the ant Oececophylla smaragdina. ‘The caterpillar number was much more on mealy bugs attended by non-aggressive ant, Anoplolepis longipes. There was an immediate improvement in the activity of S. epius and the mealy bug population was reduced considerably when ant movement was restricted. The onisci form nature of the caterpillars give them total protection from the ants because the head, legs and the soft ventral surface are completely covered by the bulging dorsal surface (Vinod Kumar et al., 2008).

heading: 4.3.33 Effect of augmentation of Spalgis epius on mealybug population
text: Release of known number of S epius caterpillars on the mealybug population on coffee plants indicated that ten to twenty caterpillars per plant were able to reduce the mealy bug population in a very short time even in the presence of attendant ants. Small numbers of the caterpillar are less likely to bring about appreciable control. The pre-release infestation of coffee plants in the selected 0.5 hectare plot was reasonably high and a random survey of the infested nodes indicated very less activity of the caterpillars of S. epius. Two releases of 450 pupae of S. epius, one at the end of February and the other during March end in the first year increased the average number of caterpillars slightly and the percentage of infested nodes decreased to some extent. Restriction of ant movement and subsequent release during the second year increased the number of caterpillars. 317 Ee a Even the pre-release estimate in the second year indicated that there was a slight improvement in the activity of S. epius than the previous year. By the month of April the predatory activity of S. epius caterpillars was much more noticeable and the percentage of infested nodes reduced considerably. This reduced level was maintained till the onset of monsoon. Overall there was a better predatory performance by S. epius due to repeated release (Vinod Kumar, et. al., 2009).

heading: 4.3.34 Survival of Leptomastix dactylopii (how) during winter season
text: The survival of L. dactylopii during the winter season in Wayanad district is reported in this paper. The parasitoids were multiplied in glass house on mealy bug infested pumpkins and field releases were made in seven Robusta coffee estates of Wayanad district in Kerala. About 25,000 parasitoids were released in a hectare plot of each estate during October 2005. The infestation level was medium (6-20 mealy bugs per node). Follow up observations were made during January 2006. The percentage parasitism of mealy bugs by L. dactylopii during winter season of Wayanad ranged from 25.34 + 5.94 to 39.68 + 3.33 with a mean of 33.63 + 4.87. It is noteworthy that L. dactylopii was able to survive the winter season and to bring about substantial control of mealy bugs. This may be due to the non severity of winter in Wayanad compared to other countries (Abdul Rahiman, et. al., 2009).

heading: 4.4.15 Effect of insecticides on Spalgis epius
text: When tested in the field using III instar caterpillars, the effect of the insecticides was acute during the first few weeks and then gradually declined, but slight effect of the insecticide could be detected even up to the 56" day after spraying, indicating the longer residual effect. Spraying of the three insecticides on mealy bug infested plants showed that on the first few days both the pest i.e. Mealy bug P citriand its natural enemy S. epius were totally eliminated from the plants. But the mealy bug population started increasing gradually by the third week of spray. There was no sign of activity of any natural enemies during this period and later. Only by about 45 days after spray a few natural enemies like the encyrtid Leptomastix dactylopii and the common coccinellid Pullus pallidicollis made their appearance on the mealy bug colony. Only after another week a few caterpillars of S. epius were noticed. This indicated that the predator S. epius was extremely sensitive to the insecticide sprays (Vinod Kumar et al., 2010).

heading: 5.3.7 Biological contro] of coffee green scale
text: During cooler months 3 i fungi attack the scale and check the buildup a Population under natural conditions, High relative humidity and low temperature are essential for the epizootics of the fungi. Of the three, Verticillium lecanii is the most effective and it causes 30-95% mortality. The fungus is also compatible with most of the insecticides even though germination of fungal spores is inhibited by insecticide. 8x10° spores/ml and Fenthion 0.1% combination is better. A surfactant may be added @ 0.5 ml/L to increase the effectiveness. During summer a humectant (Glycerol 0.1%) can be added. Addition of wetting agent during summer will increase the pathogenicity of the fungus. Use of these biological agents on coffee green scales effectively controls the pest with least disruption to the ecosystem (Rajavel et al., 1989).

heading: 5.3.8 Effect of relative humidity and temperature on the biotic agents of Green scale
text: Positive correlation was observed between relative humidity and fungal pathogen Verticillium lecanii and temperature and insect parasitoids. 325} j j Maximum percentage of infection by V. lecanii was recorded in September when high relative humidity 93% prevailed and the maximum parasitism mes noticed in May, when temperature was 32.8°C. The infections of pathogen commencing in June reaches its peak September affecting majority of the scale population and peak incidence of parasitism of scales occurs in May. The natural enemies of green scale in the field are quite active and either the pathogen or the parasitoid is continuously operating upon the pest, depending on the weather conditions. Hence any pesticide application aimed at reducing the pest should be judicious and limited only to spot application so as to have least effect on the biotic agents in the field (Bhaskara and Bhat, 1989).

heading: 8.3.2 Control of hairy caterpillars on coffee estates in South India
text: A few control measures suggested such as; (1) Set up light traps in June July to catch the adult moths during break in monsoon. (2) During July lop branches of shade trees and destroy egg masses. (3) Collect and destroy clusters of caterpillars or dust them with Folidol 1.5% dust or Metacid combi 2% dust. (4) Most effective and cheapest control measures is to collect and destroy all the pupae. (5) Digging and liming during the month of February and March. (6) Coffee and Dadap may be sprayed with Metacid combi 40 EC @ 8 Ozs/barrel of water + 1 lb. Fish-oil- resin soap or DDT + Parathion compound or BHC 50 WP at 2 Kg + 1 Ib. heading: 8.3.6 Control of Eupterote canaraica attacking coffee

heading: 8.3.7 Insecticidal control trials against Eupterote canaraica infesting coffee

Another record of the out breaks of the Pentatomid, Udonga montana Udonga montana was first recorded in 1917 from Kadur Dist. In 1953, a large number of same bugs were received from N.R. pura on the bamboo bushes. Later, it was found in large numbers on coffee bushes. When they were enclosed on potted coffee plants in field cages, they successfully bred on coffee. These attempts were failed as the number of live bugs soon dwindled and all died within about a week after enclosing them. heading: 11.31 Record of Metarhizium cylindrosporum
text: (Hypocreales: Clavicipitaceae) on Terpnosia psecas from India During a survey for entomopathogens in the coffee ecosystem, a light green fungus infecting adults of the cicada Terpnosia psecas Walker was encountered in the farm of the Central Coffee Research Institute in Chikmagalur district. Karnataka, India (13° 22M N, 750 28 E and 850 m). The cadavers of three males and one female with fungal growth were found attached to the trunks of certain shade trees during August-October 2011. Microscopic examination of the fungus revealed two types of conidia. The microconidia were ellipsoidal (3.4-6.9 x 2.3 mm) and macroconidia banana shaped (11.6-23.1 x 2.8 mm). The fungus was identified as Metarhizium cylindrosporum based on the light green colour of the conidial mass and the conidial measurements (Balakrishnan et al., 2012).

heading: 1.3 Impact of drying surface and raking frequencies on mould incidence, ochratoxin
text: A contamination and cup quality during preparation of Arabica and Robusta cherries at the farm level The aim of this study was to evaluate the impact and contribution of various drying surfaces (soil, cement, and tarpaulin) and raking frequencies (1 and 4/day) on the incidence of toxigenic molds, ochratoxin A (OTA) production, and on the overall cup quality during preparation of arabica and robusta coffee cherry in India. Two individual experimental batches (run 1 at the begin of harvest and run 2 at the end of harvest) were set up for the study. Results showed high incidence of molds in coffee dried on soil surface compared with that on cement and tarpaulin surfaces. In both arabica and robusta, OTA could be detected in Aspergillus ochraceus contaminated samples at the end of harvest. Raking of the cherries 4 times/day showed lower fungal incidence with no OTA levels detected. heading: 2.9 Relationship between sensory perceived acidity and instrumentally measured acidity in Indian coffee samples
text: A study was taken up to evaluate the relationship between the sensory perceived acidity and instrumentally measured acidity in thirteen coffee samples representing the two major commercially cultivated coffee varieties viz., Coffea arabica (arabica coffee) and C. canephora (Robusta coffee) in India. The acidity level in these coffee samples was assessed by three ways viz., organoleptic (sensory perceived) scoring, pH meter and titratable acidity. The results of this study revealed that acidity level assessed by the organoleptic scoring matched with the acidity level measured by pH meter and titratable assay method. Statistical analysis of these results indicated there was close correlation between sensory perceived acidity and instrumentally measured acidity as evidenced by the correlation coefficient (r2) value ranging from 0.86 to 0.99 (Basavaraj et al., 2014). Wet method involves a series of steps viz., pulping of ripe cherries, fermentation of depulped cherries, washing of fermented coffee, postwash soaking of washed coffee, sun drying of post-washed soaked coffee _and bagging of dried coffee. The final product of wet processing is known as dry parchment coffee.

text: Knowledge about physicomechanical and aerodynamic properties is indispensable for any crop that undergoes post-harvest processing; coffee is no exception. heading: 7.5 Incidence of toxigenic moulds in cured & uncured coffee samples
text: The presence of mycotoxins particularly Ochratoxin-A (OTA) in coffee is drawing attention of the consumers as it causes health hazard. OTA is a nephrotoxic mycotoxin classified by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) as a possible carcinogen. This toxin is known to be produced by Aspergillus ochraceus and Penicillium sp. Studies have been initiated to know the extent contamination particularly toxigenic fungi in the final product of both Arabica and Robusta coffee. As a part of the study, a survey on contamination of mould in cured and uncured samples of coffee at different curing works in Chikkamagaluru and Hassan zones was conducted. The results of the survey revealed that Aspergillus sp. was found to be predominant in all the samples (18-89%), followed by Fusarium sp. (15-43%) and yeast (17-37%). The moulds like Penicillium sp., Rhizopus sp, Mucor sp. and Cladosporium sp. were also observed in most of the samples from both the zones. The presence of toxin producing mould like A. ochraceus was found to be more in Arabica and Robusta cherry than in parchment. However, its presence was noticed in cuts, bits and black beans of both Arabica and Robusta processed by wet and dry method. In general, the frequency of A. ochraceus and Penicillium sp. recorded was high in dry processed coffee than in wet processed coffee (Panneerselvam et al., 2000).

heading: 7.6 Coffee husk - A _ potential source of ochratoxin- A contamination
text: Solid wastes from coffee processing, e.g. parchment and cherry husks of ‘Arabica’ and ‘Robusta’ varieties were tested for the presence of ochratoxin A (OTA), a mycotoxin produced by aii Aspergillus ochraccus and Penicillium verrucosut. The cherry husk of ‘Robusta’ had relatively higher level of OTA, ranging from 7.9 to 53.0 ppb compared to 3.6 to 18.0 ppb in ‘Arabica cherry husk. In the parchment of ‘Robusta’ and ‘Arabica there was no significant difference in the OTA. The results indicated that the coffee husk can be a potential source of OTA; hence, effective separation and immediate disposal of these wastes are of paramount importance to minimize the OTA contamination in coffee products (Gopinandhan et al., 2006).

heading: 7.7 The occurrence of ochratoxin-A in green and commercial coffee samples
text: A total of 148 coffee samples were tested for the natural occurrence of ochratoxin-A (OT-A). Among these, 100 (68%) and 19 (13%) samples had OT-A contamination of 0.1-1.0 ppb, and 1.1-5.0 ppb, respectively and 3 samples had> 5 ppb. The highest level of OT-A contamination was 11.7 ppb in a ‘Robusta’ cherry. The results indicated that majority of the Indian coffee samples analyzed that contained insignificant level of OT-A (Gopinandhan et al., 2007).

heading: 7.13 Effect of roasting and brewing on stability of ochratoxin A in coffee k
text: Effect of roasting and filter brewing on the stability of ochratoxin A (OTA) was studied using 3 naturally contaminated and 2 artificially infected coffee bean (Coffea canephora) samples. The OTA contaminated coffee samples were subjected to roasting temperatures of 180, 200 and 220°C, roasting levels of light, medium and dark, brewing times of 7, 15 and 20 min and analyzed for OTA content following immuno affinity column cleanup procedure coupled with high performance liquid chromatography. Naturally contaminated coffee samples showed OTA reduction from 4 to 36.8% with an average of 22%. Artificially infected coffee sample showed OTA reduction from 7 to 28.3% with an average of 16.6%. The filter method of coffee brewing reduced OTA content by 14% (Gopinandhan et al., 2009). Coffee berry borer (CBB, Hypothenemus etc canteen apm en psn gece CR ren AR me i enn Papers) (Abstracts of Rese: 379 hampei Ferrari) is a common insect pest in coffee plantations and is a suspected vector of various mycotoxin- producing molds. In the present study, field trials were undertaken consecutively for 3 years to evaluate the impact of CBB on the microbial contamination of Arabica and Robusta coflee bean varieties, with emphasis laid toward ochratoxin-A (OTA) producing fungi. Results revealed higher microbial contamination in CBBinfested beans in both the varieties of coffee with the presence of toxigenic molds (such as Aspergillus niger, Aspergillus ochraceus). The “timely harvested” coftee, which was infested with CBB, was found to possess comparatively lesser OTA levels than those berries left in soil or on coffee plants. Studies carried out on coftee beans collected from nine curing factories indicated the presence of OTA in almost all the CBB-infested coffee beans, irrespective of the variety. Results of the present study provide sufficient baseline information and evidence to understand and correlate the role of CBB with various OTA-producing molds in coffee beans. Understanding the role of CBB might be useful and applicable in the coffee-growing regions of the world, especially in plantations for production of quality coffee (Velmourougane et al., 2010).

Currently, the effluent treatment plant (ETP) module developed by Central Coffee Research Institute (CCRI) in collaboration with National Environmental Engineering Research Institute (NEERI) during 1980 is employed for treating the coffee effluent. text: The new process is concerned only with the second step in the preparation of coffee for the market freeing the coffee bean from the pecticgel coat that surrounds it. Essentially, the new method calls merely for substituting the action of caustic soda for the natural bacterial action in the fermentation process. In the new chemical process, green-coffee weight losses are greatly reduced because of the rapidity of the process it takes less than an hour to free the coffee beans from their cover of gel. The seed does not have enough time to transform its solids into gases. During 195152 season, when > 430,000 pounds of coffee berries was chemically processed in El Salvador, yield gains ranged from 1 to 3%. It requires no elaborate equipment. Caustic soda costs little. The chemically digested pectin can be recovered as a by-product, which would increase the profits of the coffee curing industry. It will have fuller flavour and aroma and less variation in quality from pound to pound (Hansen, 1953).

Then chances of fungal contamination are more in coffee berries dried on mud floor than in those dried on clean concrete/tiled floor. Ochratoxins have been known to occur in a variety of foods. heading: 2.45 Speciality coffees
text: Speciality coffees are high quality coffees and are different from that of normal coffees with reference to visual quality, in cup or in both. Speciality coffees are produced and processed with great care to preserve the intrinsic quality of the beans. Specialty coffees are growing in the world coffee market and they are fetching an attractive premium over that of normal coffees. Specialty coffees can be broadly classified into six categories based on their unique features. 1) Flavoured coffees, 2) Decaffeinated coffees, 3) Organic coffee, 4) Estate coffee, 5) Varietal coffee, 6) Indian Specialty coffee and 7) The monsooned coffee (Basavaraj et al., 1998).

heading: 2.46 Quality improvement of coffee through irradiation-prospects
text: Among the alternate methods, gamma- irriadiation has been effectively used to preserve the quality of food including green coffee beans. Exposure of coffee beans to gamma radiation being a cold process, helps in preserving coffee flavour, besides helping in shelf life extension. Studies on the effect of irradiation on monsooned coffee beans might help in working out the mechanism for improved flavour of monsooned coffee. Both low and high doses of gamma rays could be employed to improve the quality beans. While low doses of gamma rays help in controlling the coffee weevil proliferation, high doses of gamma rays might result in the enhancement of coffee aroma by activating aroma precursors. heading: 57 Microencapsulation of antioxidant phenolic compounds from green coffee
text: Green coffee is a prime source of antioxidants unctional food and nutraceuticals. Arabica and usta varieties were screened and decaffeinated g ethyl lactate and extracted with a polar ent to obtain chlorogenic acid (CGA) enriched n coffee extract (GCE). The physicochemical qualities (moisture, pH, particle size, and color) and bioactive compounds (total phenolics, chlorogenic acid, and caffeine) of GCE were assessed. ‘The GCE had 12.78 + 2.1 mg GAE gl phenolics and 10.98 mg gl chlorogenic acid (CGA). To improve the stability of CGA, the GCE encapsulated by spray drying using maltodextrin (MD) and skim milk (SM) as coating agent individually and in combination. Physicochemical, antioxidant properties, and bio functionalities of micro particles were evaluated. Highest encapsulation efficiency of GCE with maltodextrin (1:1) was 86%+3 with the smaller particle size (2.3 + 0.1 mm). heading: 2.58 Coffee starter microbiome and in-silico approach to improve Arabica coffee
text: Arabica coffee is fermented to obtain intense flavor profile and finds elusive prospects in the coffee industry. The Arabica coffee mucilage constitute 2-5% of the fruit dry weight with 94% moisture, 4% sugar, 0.7% protein and 1-3% pectin. Inductive isolation and screening of functional attributes of microbial strains were examined. Fermentative vigor along with the enzymatic progression of the microbes was streamlined and the potential isolates of consortia were optimized. The In-silico docking studies on the fermentation mechanism evidenced minimal interaction between Pectin and pectinase at lower energy level. The 1CZF disclose the best interaction binding energy (—3.92 kJ/mol) with rapid enzymatic and desired fermentation. A CCRD was employed to study the interactive effect of isolates. The consortia of Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Lactobacillus plantarum and Bacillus sphaericus (1:1:1) at 10% inoculum concentration found significant in demucilizatin of coffee beans with noticeable improvement in alcohol (70.26 mg/ ml), sugar (5.5 mg/ml) and pectinase (11.66 U/ml) compared to natural fermentation. The sensory TONAL, DEVERAGL, BREWING PHIST( profile of starter fermentation (G) scored 7.0 on 1-10 scale. Prospective insights on application of sturter consortia on Arabica coffee fermentation indicates prime requisite for cofiee industry (Siri Devi et al., 2019).

heading: 5 Carbohydrates of different components of ripe fruits in coffee
text: Reducing, non-reducing, total sugars and starch contents were determined in fruit wall (pulp), mucilage and seed of fully ripe fruits of Kents, 5.795, §.1934, S.274 and C. dewevrei var excelsa plants. heading: 14 Production and characterization of biochar from crop residues of coffee plantation and coffee processing wastes

heading: 23 Cost of production of Robusta coffee in major
text: §rowing regions of India The findings on cost of production of robusta coffee in major growing regions of India indicated that the average cost of production per hectare is Rs. 38.775 in Chikkamagaluru. Rs. 40.096 in Kodagu and Rs. 36,994 in Kerala. However, the cost per Kg was low in Kodagu (Rs. 21 per Kg) followed by Chikkamagaluru (Rs. 27 per Kg) and Kerala (Rs. 31 per Kg) because of varied yield realizations (1922 Kg/ha, 1435 Kg/ha and 1203 Kg/ha respectively). Further, the analysis revealed that an average yield gap of 830 Kg/ha in Chikkamagaluru. 631Kg/ha in Kodagu and 527 Kg/ha in Kerala were observed between irrigated and non-irrigated holdings. Thus, bridging the yield gaps either through irrigation or better management practices between the regions as well as irrigated and non-irrigated holdings of different regions to potential levels will boost the productivity levels of robusta, which reduces the cost of production per unit of output (Babu Reddy et al., 2001).

heading: 24 Estimation of cost of production of Arabica coffee in Chikkamagaluru region, Karnataka
text: A study was carried out to estimate the cost of production of Arabica coffee in Chikkamagaluru region covering 63 estates consisting of holdings with different sizes by adopting a multistage random sampling method. The results indicated that the average total cost of cultivation of Arabica (Abstracts of Research Pzpers) coffee in Chikkamagaluru region was Rs. 52,955 per ha which translated into a cost of production of Rs. 51 per kg with an average yield realization of 1040 kg/ha. Among the total cost, labour cost alone accounted for 54% followed by input cost (30%) and overhead expenditure (16%). While, across the holding size groups, the cost of cultivation was high in 4 to 10 hectare category with Rs. 55,450 per ha, followed by Rs. 54,790 (10-40 ha), Rs. 53,400 (> 40 ha) and Rs. 48.045 (4 ha) and per unit cost of production worked out to be Rs. 47 per kg (<4 ha.). Rs 51 per kg (410 ha). Rs. 49 per kg (10-40 ha and Rs, 53 per kg (> 40 ha), which was reflected mainly by varied yield realizations and the cost components. The yield realizations were 1020 kg/ ha (<4 ha), 1085 kg/ha (4-10 ha). 1125 kg/ha (1040 ha) and 1015 kg/ha (> 40 ha) indicating a yield gap of 110 kg/ha among the different size holding groups.

heading: 20 Coffee certificntion in India: Awareness, practices, and sustainability perception of prowers
text: Certification programs have been employed in many apricultural products as a means to encourage and communicate compliance with standards associated with various attributes, such as organic, fair-trade, GMO free and eco-friendly among others. Such programs further seek to provide added value, through a price premium, to producers and supply chain actors associated with the label. In this paper, we review a number of global labeling and certification programs that could add value for coffee farms in India through the promotion of conservation and environmental protection. We provide results from a survey conducted ona sample of coflee farms in Coorg district, India, to assess their awareness and perceptions related toward certified coffee and environmental conservation in general. Survey results illustrate strong positive associations with the environment by coffee planters, particularly among certified and organic producers. However, price premiums for certified and organic coffee are relatively small.

heading: 20 Coffee certificntion in India: Awareness, practices, and sustainability perception of prowers
text: We provide results from a survey conducted ona sample of coflee farms in Coorg district, India, to assess their awareness and perceptions related toward certified coffee and environmental conservation in general. Survey results illustrate strong positive associations with the environment by coffee planters, particularly among certified and organic producers. However, price premiums for certified and organic coffee are relatively small. While the potential of conservation-oriented certification for coffee in Coorg could be relatively limited outside of a few individual-level niches, branding Coorg more generally as a conservation-oriented region could hold promise, leveraging and personalizing the uniqueness of the natural offerings from Coorg and tapping into burgeoning associations with place and region in India (Rich et al., 2018).

The production and yield of coffee had increased in all the major coffee producing countries from pre-liberalization to post liberalization period. The area had decreased in Brazil and Colombia but in other countries including India the area had increased in both the periods. The stability of the area, production and productivity remains unstable (>20%) over the years in the countries including India however the instability started to decline (15-20%) in the postliberalization period.
